(MF.) One says yawomu SarodK and ↓ SaradK [ A day of cold: or of intense cold ]. (M, A, L.) -A3- See also SuradN , near the end.

sourceDefinition: A certain bird, (S, M, K,) above the size of the sparrow, (M,) having a large head, (K,) which preys upon sparrows: (T, K:) a certain bird, black and white, or party-coloured, ( A^aboqaEu ,) with a white belly: (A:) a certain bird of the crow-kind, also called AlwaAqiY : (Msb:) the Arabs used to regard its cry, (L, Msb,) and the bird itself, (L,) as of evil omen, (L, Msb,) and used to kill it; and they are forbidden to kill it, in order to dispel the idea of a thing's being of evil omen: (Msb:) there are two species thereof; one species is called by the people of El-'Irák AlEaqoEaqu [a name now applied to the magpie, corvus pica ]; the other species, called AlS~uradu AlhamohaAmu , [so in the L, but in my copy of the Msb AlhyAm ,] is the wild sort, which is found in Nejd, upon the trees called EiDaAh ; it is never seen but upon the ground, [so in the L, but in my copy of the Msb, it is never seen upon the ground, ] springing from tree to tree: (Sukeyn En-Numeyree, L, Msb:) when chased, and hard pressed, it is overtaken, and utters a cry like that of the hawk: it preys upon sparrows: (Msb:) it is described by AHát as a bird black and white, or party-coloured, ( A^aboqaEu ,) with a white belly, and a back of a dark, or an ashy, dust-colour ( A^axoDar ), [or, as is said in the L, half white and half black, found in trees, ] large in the head and beak, having a talon with which it preys upon sparrows and other small birds, as large as the point of a spear: (Mgh, Msb:) some add to this that it is called Almujaw~afu , because of the whiteness of its belly; and AlA^axoTabu , because of the dark, or ashy, dust-colour of its back; and AlA^axoyalu [a name now applied to the green woodpecker, picus viridis ], because of its diversity of colour; that it is never seen but upon a branch ( fiY $uEobapK , and so in the L,) or a tree, (Mgh, Msb,) and can scarcely ever, or never, be taken, (Msb,) or can never be taken: (Mgh, L:) it is regarded as of evil omen: (Mgh:) Sgh says that it is called sumayoTN , [perhaps a mistranscription for $umayoTN , because black and white,] in the dim. form: (Msb:) [it is said that] it was the first bird that fasted for the sake of God: (K:) the pl. is SirodaAnN : (S, M, Msb, K:) and the female is called SuradapN . (Msb.) ― -b2- Also (tropical:) A white place, (S, M, L, K,) produced by galls, (S, L, K,) or by the saddle; (M;) or SuradapN signifies a white place produced by hair growing in the place of a gall; likened to the colour of the bird thus called: (A:) pl. SirodaAnN . (M, A.) And (assumed tropical:) A white place on the hump of a camel: (M:) or white fur growing in the place of a gall produced by the saddle, after its healing: (AO:) pl. as above. (AO, M.) ― -b3- And (assumed tropical:) A certain vein (As, M) beneath the tongue, (As,) or in the lower part of the tongue, (M,) of the horse. (As, M.) And AlS~uradaAni (assumed tropical:) Two veins, (Lth, Ks, S, M, L, K,) of a dark, or an ashy, dust-colour, ( A^axoDaraAni , Lth, Ks, M, L,) in the lower part of the tongue, by means of which the tongue moves about, (Lth, Ks, L,) or penetrating within ( yasotaboTinaAni ) the tongue: (S, M, K:) or two veins, on the right and left of the tongue: (L:) or, as some say, two bones, which erect ( yuqiymaAni ) the tongue. (M.) Yezeed Ibn-Es- Sa'ik in his saying lahu SuradaAni munoTaliqaA All~isaAni means *aribaAni [i. e. *aribaA All~isaAni , for *aribN lisaAnuhumaA , as though he said lahu lisaAnN *aribN He has a long, or an unbridled, tongue; the phrase that he uses being pleonastic]. (S.) ― -b4- Also, (M, L,) or ↓ SarodN , (so in the K,) and ↓ SaradN , which is the more known, (TA,) A nail in a spear-head, (M, L, K,) by means of which the shaft is fastened to it. (L, K. *) ― -b5- Accord. to Sh, fat~aHa Suradahu means He opened his mind, so as to reveal his secrets. (TA. [But this is perhaps a mistranscription, for ftH Surarahu : see Sur~apN .])

the other species, called AlS~uradu AlhamohaAmu , [so in the L, but in my copy of the Msb AlhyAm ,] is the wild sort, which is found in Nejd, upon the trees called EiDaAh ; it is never seen but upon the ground, [so in the L, but in my copy of the Msb, it is never seen upon the ground, ] springing from tree to tree: (Sukeyn En-Numeyree, L, Msb:) when chased, and hard pressed, it is overtaken, and utters a cry like that of the hawk: it preys upon sparrows: (Msb:) it is described by AHát as a bird black and white, or party-coloured, ( A^aboqaEu ,) with a white belly, and a back of a dark, or an ashy, dust-colour ( A^axoDar ), [or, as is said in the L, half white and half black, found in trees, ] large in the head and beak, having a talon with which it preys upon sparrows and other small birds, as large as the point of a spear: (Mgh, Msb:) some add to this that it is called Almujaw~afu , because of the whiteness of its belly; and AlA^axoTabu , because of the dark, or ashy, dust-colour of its back; and AlA^axoyalu [a name now applied to the green woodpecker, picus viridis ], because of its diversity of colour; that it is never seen but upon a branch ( fiY $uEobapK , and so in the L,) or a tree, (Mgh, Msb,) and can scarcely ever, or never, be taken, (Msb,) or can never be taken: (Mgh, L:) it is regarded as of evil omen: (Mgh:) Sgh says that it is called sumayoTN , [perhaps a mistranscription for $umayoTN , because black and white,] in the dim. form: (Msb:) [it is said that] it was the first bird that fasted for the sake of God: (K:) the pl. is SirodaAnN : (S, M, Msb, K:) and the female is called SuradapN . (Msb.) ― -b2- Also (tropical:) A white place, (S, M, L, K,) produced by galls, (S, L, K,) or by the saddle; (M;) or SuradapN signifies a white place produced by hair growing in the place of a gall; likened to the colour of the bird thus called: (A:) pl. SirodaAnN . (M, A.) And (assumed tropical:) A white place on the hump of a camel: (M:) or white fur growing in the place of a gall produced by the saddle, after its healing: (AO:) pl. as above. (AO, M.) ― -b3- And (assumed tropical:) A certain vein (As, M) beneath the tongue, (As,) or in the lower part of the tongue, (M,) of the horse. (As, M.) And AlS~uradaAni (assumed tropical:) Two veins, (Lth, Ks, S, M, L, K,) of a dark, or an ashy, dust-colour, ( A^axoDaraAni , Lth, Ks, M, L,) in the lower part of the tongue, by means of which the tongue moves about, (Lth, Ks, L,) or penetrating within ( yasotaboTinaAni ) the tongue: (S, M, K:) or two veins, on the right and left of the tongue: (L:) or, as some say, two bones, which erect ( yuqiymaAni ) the tongue. (M.) Yezeed Ibn-Es- Sa'ik in his saying lahu SuradaAni munoTaliqaA All~isaAni means *aribaAni [i. e. *aribaA All~isaAni , for *aribN lisaAnuhumaA , as though he said lahu lisaAnN *aribN He has a long, or an unbridled, tongue; the phrase that he uses being pleonastic]. (S.) ― -b4- Also, (M, L,) or ↓ SarodN , (so in the K,) and ↓ SaradN , which is the more known, (TA,) A nail in a spear-head, (M, L, K,) by means of which the shaft is fastened to it. (L, K. *) ― -b5- Accord. to Sh, fat~aHa Suradahu means He opened his mind, so as to reveal his secrets. (TA. [But this is perhaps a mistranscription, for ftH Surarahu : see Sur~apN .])

sourceDefinition: [The hawk; ] the bird with which one hunts, or catches, game; (S;) whatever preys, or hunts or catches game, of the birds called buziAp [pl. of baAzK ] and $awaAhiyn [pl. of $aAhiyn ]; (M, A, K;) a kind of bird including the baAziY and the $aAhiyn and the zur~aq and the yuw^oyuw^ and the baA$aq : (AHát, TA in art. b$q :) [like our term “ saker, ” and the French “ sacre, ” &c:] pl. [of pauc.] A^aSoqurN (M, K) and [of mult.] SuquwrN and SuquwrapN (M, A, K) and SiqaArN and SiqaArapN and SuqurN ; (M, K;) the last of which is said by Th to be pl. of SuquwrN , which is pl. of SaqorN , but [ISd says] I hold it to be pl. of SaqorN : the fem. is ↓ SaqorapN . (M.) ― -b2- [And accord. to Reiske, as mentioned by Freytag, A liberal man: perhaps a noble man, as likened to a hawk.] -A2- Also, (S, K,) and ↓ SaqorapN , (S, M, K,) Vehemence of the stroke of the sun, (S, M, K,) and fierceness of its heat: (M:) or the vehemence of its stroke upon the head: (M:) pl. [of the latter] SaqaraAtN . (S, A.) -A3- Also the former, Sour milk; (K;) [and] so ↓ SaqorapN : (A:) or milk rendered sour by a stroke of the sun: (Sh:) or milk sour in the utmost degree: (As:) or very sour milk; as also ↓ SaqorapN : (S:) or this latter is milk that has curdled, and of which the thick part has become separate, and the whey become clear, and that has become sour, so as to be a good kind of sauce. (L.) One says, tazowiY Alwajoha ↓ jaA='anaA biSaqorapK [ He brought us some sour milk, or very sour milk, &c., such as contracts the face, or makes it to wrinkle: like as one says biSarobapK ]. sourceDefinition: [ Wool; ] an appertenance of sheep, (in the S lil$~aApi , in the M liloganami , and in the O and Msb [more definitely] lilD~aA^oni ,) which is to them like $aEarN to goats and wabarN to camels: (M:) [in the K only said to be well know:] n. un. SuwfapN , (M,) [i. e.] this latter has a more particular signification [meaning a portion, flock, tuft, or wisp, of wool ]: (S, O, Msb, K:) and sometimes SuwfN is used in the sense of the n. un., as mentioned by Sb: (M:) the pl. of SuwfN is A^aSowaAfN [meaning sorts of wool ]: (M:) and the dim. of the n. un. is ↓ SuwayofapN . (TA.) One says xaroqaA='u wajadato SuwfFA [ An unskilful woman that has found wool ]: (As, O, K:) a prov. (As, O) relating to property possessed by such as does not deserve to have it: (As, TA:) because the unskilful woman, when she lights upon wool, mars it, (O, K,) not spinning it well: (O:) applied to the stupid person who finds property and wastes it; (O, K;) or to him who finds that of which he knows not the value, and wastes it. (Z, TA.) And one says, fulaAnN yalobasu AlS~uwfa waAlquTona , meaning Such a one wears what is made of wool and of cotton. (A, TA.) In the saying of a poet, HalobaAnapK rakobaAnapK Safuwfi taxoliTu bayona wabarK waSuwfi [ Of one that is milked and ridden, that yields a row of bowls of her milk, (but see SafuwfN , of which other explanations have been given,) that mingles camels' fur and wool ], the latter hemistich means, as Th says, accord. to IAar, that is sold, and with the price whereof are purchased camels and sheep: or, accord. to As, that is quick in her pace; the drawing back of her fore legs being likened to [the motion of] the bow of the nad~aAf who mixes camels' fur and wool. (M.) One says also, A^axa*otu biSuwfi raqabatihi (S, M, K, but in the M A^axa*a ,) and biSuwfatihaA (M, O) and ↓ biSaAfihaA , (M, K,) and biTuwfi raqabatihi and biTaAfihaA , and biZuwfi zaqabatihi and biZaAfihaA , and biquwfi raqabatihi and biqaAfihaA , (S, O,) meaning (tropical:) [ I laid hold upon ] the pendent hair in the hollow of the back of his neck: (IDrd, S, M, O, K:) or the downy hairs upon the back of his neck: (M, O:) or the skin of his neck: (IAar, S, O, K:) or the back of his neck, altogether: (Fr, S, O, K:) or I took him by force: (Abu-l-Ghowth, S, O, K:) or I followed him, thinking that I should not reach him, and overtook him; and this one says whether he lay hold upon his neck or not. (Abu-s-Semeyda', S, O, K.) And A^aEoTaAhu biSuwfi raqabatihi (tropical:) [ He gave it altogether ]; like A^aEoTaAhu birum~atihi : or (as expl. by A' Obeyd, S, O) he gave it gratuitously; not taking a price. (S, O, K.) ― -b2- Suwfu AlbaHori [lit. The wool of the sea ] is a thing [or substance ] in the form of the animal Suwf [i. e., of wool; evidently meaning sea-weed resembling wool; such as is found in abundance thrown up on the beaches of the Red Sea: and that this is generally, if not in every instance, meant by the identical Hebrew word סוּף , as used in the Bible, has been most satisfactorily shown in art. “ Red Sea ” (by my deeply-lamented nephew Edward Stanley Poole) in Dr. William Smith's “ Dictionary of the Bible ”]: it is said in one of the A^abadiy~aAt , [see art. Abd ,] laA A=tiyka maA bal~a baHorN SuwfapF [ I will not come to thee as long as a sea wets a portion of Suwf ], or, as Lh relates it, maA bal~a AlbaHoru Suwfahu [ as long as the sea wets its Suwf ; meaning, ever ]. (M, TA.)

DaraAwapN (S, M, Msb, K) and DarFA (M, Msb, K) and DaroYN and DaraA='apN , (K, TA, [the last in the CK written DaraAp ,]) He was, or became, attached, addicted, or devoted, to it; (S, M, K, TA;) and (TA) he habituated, or accustomed, himself to it, (M, * Msb, K, * TA,) so that he could hardly, or in nowise, withhold himself from it; (TA;) and emboldened himself to do it or undertake it or the like: and he kept, or clave, to it; and became attached, addicted, or devoted, to it; like the animal of prey to the chase. (Msb.) [And Dariyahu occurs in the M, in art. mrs , in explanation of tamar~asa bihi , app. for DariYa bihi , in the same sense.] It is said in a trad., A_in~a liloA_isolaAmi DaraAwapF i. e. Verily there is a habituating and an attachment of oneself to El-Islám; meaning, one cannot withhold himself from it. (TA.) And in a saying, (S,) or trad., (M, TA,) of 'Omar, A_iy~aAkumo wah`*ihi AlmajaAzira faA_in~a lahaA DaraAwapF kaDaraAwapi Alxamori (S, M, TA) i. e. [ Avoid ye these places where cattle are slaughtered and where their flesh is sold, for ] there is a habituating of oneself to them, and a yearning towards them, like the habituating of oneself to wine; for he who habituates himself to flesh-meat hardly, or in nowise, withholds himself from it, and becomes extravagant in his expenditure. (TA. [See also majozarN .]) And one says of a dog, DariYa biAlS~ayodi , (S, M, Mgh, K,) [in Har p. 579 fY AlSayd , which I do not find elsewhere,] aor. , (S,) inf. n. And Dariyati Aljar~apu biAlxal~i [ The jar became seasoned with vinegar ] and biAln~abiy*i [ with must or the like ]. (TA.) And DariYa Aln~abiy*u The nby* became strong [by remaining several days in the jar or skin]. (TA.) -A2- DaraA , (S, K,) aor. , inf. n. DarowN , (S,) or Duruw~N , (K,) said of a vein, It shed blood: (S, K:) or, accord. to the T, it quivered, and gushed with blood or made a sound by reason of the blood coming forth: Z says that the form of the verb is altered because of the alteration of the meaning. (TA.) And DaraY , (M, K,) aor. , (K,) [likewise] said of a vein, (M,) signifies It flowed, (M, K, TA,) and ran [ with blood ]; on the authority of IAar. (TA.) And DaraA , aor. , said of a wound, It ceased not to flow [ with blood ]. (IAth, TA.) -A3- And DaraA , inf. n. Drw [whether DarowN or Duruw~N is not shown], said of a man, He hid, or concealed, himself. (IKtt, TA. [See also 10.])

definition: A dog, (M,) or young dog, (S, Kudot;
sourceDefinition: A dog, (M,) or young dog, (S, Kudot;,) such as is termed DaArK [i. e. habituated, or accustomed, to the chase ]; (S, M, K;) as also ↓ DariY~N : (K, TA: [in the CK, kAlD~araY is erroneously put for kaAlD~ariY~i :]) the latter word is like ganiY~N : (TA:) the fem. of the former is with p : and the pl. [of pauc.] A^aDorK [originally A^aDoruwN ] and [of mult.] DiraA='N . (S, M.) -A2- And A taint of ju*aAm [or elephantiasis]: (M, K:) occurring in a trad. in which it is said of Aboo-Bekr, A^akala maEa rajulK bihi DirowN mino ju*aAmK [ He ate with a man in whom was a taint of elephantiasis ]: it is from [the inf. n.] AlD~araAwapu ; as though the disease became attached, or habituated, to the person: (M, TA:) mentioned by Hr in the “ Ghareebeyn: ” (M:) or, as some relate it, the word is with the fet-h, [i. e. ↓ DarowN ,] and is from DaraA said of a wound, the meaning being in whom was a wound having an incessant flowing. (TA.) -A3- Also, and ↓ DarowN , A species of tree, of sweet odour, with [ the wood of ] which the teeth are rubbed and cleansed, and the leaves of which are put into perfume; (M, TA;) i. q. maHolabN [q. v.]; so says Lth: (TA:) AHn says, the places of its growth are mostly in ElYemen; (M, TA;) and some say that the Dirow is the buTom [or terebinth-tree, or the fruit thereof ]: (M:) AHn says also, it is of the trees of the mountains, and is like the great oak, (M, TA, *) having clusters [ of berries ] like those of the oak, but its berries are larger; its leaves are cooked, and, when thoroughly cooked, are cleared away, and the water thereof is returned to the fire, and coagulates, (M, TA,) becoming like qubayoTaA=' [q. v.], (M,) and is used medicinally as a remedy for roughness of the chest and for pain of the fauces: (M, TA:) or the gum of a certain tree called the kamokaAm [i. e. the cancamum-tree ], brought from El-Yemen: (S:) or this is a mistake, for it is the tree so called, not its gum: (K:) [but] it is said in the T, on the authority of AHn, that kamokaAm signifies the bark ( qirof ) of the tree called Dirow : and some say that it is the resin ( Eilok ) of the Dirow : and in the Moheet of Ibn-'Abbád it is said that kamokaAm signifies the bark ( qirof , or, as some say, liHaA=' ,) of the tree called Dirow , and is an aromatic perfume: (TA:) and (K, TA) IAar says, (TA,) the Dirow is the Hab~ap xaDoraA=' [or fruit of the terebinth-tree ], (K, TA,) which is also sometimes used for rubbing and cleansing the teeth: when a girl rubs and cleanses her teeth with a stick of the tree called Dirow the saliva with which the stick is moistened from her mouth is like honey: (TA:) and the word is also pronounced ↓ DarowN . (K.)

definition: A level tract of land in which are beasts of prey and a few trees: (M, K:) or a piece of land, or ground, that conceals one: (AA, TA:) and trees, &c.
sourceDefinition: A level tract of land in which are beasts of prey and a few trees: (M, K:) or a piece of land, or ground, that conceals one: (AA, TA:) and trees, &c., that conceal one: (M:) or a thicket; or tangled, or luxuriant, or abundant and dense, trees; in a valley. (S, K.) One says, tawaAraY AlS~ayodu min~iY fiY DaraA='i AlwaAdiY [ The game hid itself from me in the tangled, or luxuriant, or abundant and dense, trees of the valley ]. (S.) And fulaAnN yamo$iY AlD~araA='a , with fet-h, meaning Such a one goes along lurking among the trees that conceal him. (S.) And huwa yadib~u lahu AlD~araA='a wayamo$iY lahu Alxamara [ He creeps to him in the thicket, and walks, or goes along, to him in the covert of trees ]: said of a man when he deludes, or circumvents, his companion: (S:) but accord. to IAar, DrA=' here means a low, or depressed, place. (Meyd.) And fulaAnN laA yudab~u lahu AlD~araA='u [app. meaning The thicket will not be crept through to such a one: but mentioned after the last of the explanations here following]. (M.) [See also Dar~aA='u , in art. Dr .] ― -b2- [It is said that] it signifies also The hiding or concealing, oneself: (AA, K, TA:) [or] the walking, or going along, in that which conceals one from him whom one beguiles, or circumvents. (M.)

definition: Attached, addicted, or devoted, to a thing;
sourceDefinition: Attached, addicted, or devoted, to a thing; (TA;) habituated, or accustomed, thereto, (Msb, TA,) so as hardly, or in nowise, to withhold himself therefrom; (TA;) and emboldening himself to do it or undertake it or the like: and keeping, or cleaving, thereto; being attached, addicted, or devoted, to it; like the animal of prey to the chase. (Msb.) [Hence,] kalobN DaArK , (S, Mgh,) or kalobN DaArK biAlS~ayodi , (M, K,) A dog habituated, or accustomed, to the chase: (S, Mgh, TA:) and kalobapN DaAriyapN . (S. [See also DirowN , first sentence.]) [ kalobN DaArK biAlS~ayodi is also expl. in the TA by the words A_i*aA taTaE~ama bilaHomihi , app. meaning A dog having his appetite excited by tasting the flesh of the game. ] DawaArK [is pl. of DaArK applied to an irrational animal, and as such] signifies [ Animals accustomed to prey; rapacious, or ravenous, beasts; and particularly] lions. (TA.) And AlmawaA$iY AlD~aAriyapu The cattle that are in the habit of pasturing upon peoples' seed-produce. (Nh, TA.) And bayotN DaArK biAll~aHomi A house, or tent, in which flesh-meat is habitually found so much that its odour remains in it. (TA.) And siqaA='N DaArK biAll~abani , thus correctly, as in the M, but in [some of] the copies of the K biAls~amoni , (TA,) A skin in which milk is long kept so that its flavour becomes good. (M, TA.) And jar~apN DaAriyapN biAlxal~i and biAln~abiy*i [ A jar become seasoned with vinegar and with must or the like ]. (M, TA.) AlA_inaA='u AlD~aAriY , occurring in a trad. of 'Alee, is said to mean The jar that runs [or leaks ]; and the drinking from it is forbidden because it renders the drinking troublesome: thus expl. by IAar: but it is also expl. as meaning the wine-jar that has become seasoned with wine ( DariYa biAloxamori ); so that when nabiy* is put into it, it becomes intoxicating. (TA.) And EiroqN DaArK means A vein shedding blood: (S, K, TA:) [or quivering, and gushing with blood or making a sound by reason of the blood coming forth: (see the verb:)] or flowing, or running: (TA: see DariY~N :) or accustomed to be opened, and therefore when the time for it is come and it is opened, emitting its blood more quickly. (TA.)

definition: and ↓ DiloEN , (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K,) the former of the dial.
sourceDefinition: and ↓ DiloEN , (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K,) the former of the dial. of El-Hijáz and the latter of the dial. of Temeem, (Msb, TA,) and ↓ DaloEN , which is the only form, or almost the only one, that is used by the vulgar, is said by MF to be mentioned by some one or more of the commentators, but not known in the lexicons, (TA;) [ A rib; ] a certain appertenance of an animal, (Msb,) well known; (K;) the curved thing of the side; (TA;) a single bone of the bones of the side: (Mgh, Msb:) of the fem. gender, (Msb, K, TA,) accord. to common repute; or, as some say, masc.; or, accord. to some, whose opinion in this case is preferred by Ibn-Málik and others, of both genders: (TA:) pl. [of mult.] DuluwEN and [of pauc.] A^aDolaAEN (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K) and A^aDoluEN , (O, Msb, K,) and A^aDaAliEu also is a pl. of DilaEN , or, as some say, of [its pl.] A^aDoluEN . (TA.) DilaEu Alxalofi [and Alxilofi ] is [ The rib ] in the lowest part of the side [of a man, i. e. the lowest rib; and the hindmost rib in a beast]: (TA:) and signifies also A burn in the part behind what is thus termed. (O, K, TA.) ― -b2- Also (assumed tropical:) A piece of stick or wood; syn. EuwdN ; [erroneously supposed by Golius and Freytag to mean here the musical instrument thus called;] (IAar, O, K;) so in a saying of the Prophet to a woman, respecting a blood-stain on a garment, Hut~iyhi biDilaEK (assumed tropical:) [ Scrape thou it off with a piece of stick ]: (IAar, O:) or (assumed tropical:) such as is wide and curved; as being likened to the DilaE (O, K) of an animal. (K.) ― -b3- And (tropical:) An oblong piece of a melon; (O, * K, TA;) as being likened to the DilaE [properly thus called]. (O, TA.) ― -b4- And (tropical:) A trap for birds; because of its gibbous shape: so in the saying, naSaba DilaEFA lilT~ayori [ He set up a trap for the birds ]. (A, TA.) ― -b5- And The base, or lower part, of a raceme of a palm-tree. (TA in art. Ehn .) ― -b6- And (assumed tropical:) A line that is made on the ground, after which another line is made, and then the space between these two is sown. (TA.) ― -b7- And (assumed tropical:) A small mountain apart from others: (S, O, K:) or a small mountain, such as is not long: (TA:) or a low and narrow mountain, (Aboo-Nasr, S, O, K, TA,) long and extended: or, accord. to As, a small mountain, extending lengthwise upon the earth, not high. (TA.) And [the pl.] DuluwEN signifies (tropical:) Curved tracts of ground: or tracks ( TaraAy^iq ) of a [ piece of stony ground such as is termed ] Har~ap . (O, K, TA.) ― -b8- Also (assumed tropical:) An island in the sea; pl. A^aDolaAEN : or, as some say, it is the name of a particular island. (TA.) ― -b9- [In geometry, (assumed tropical:) A side of a rectilinear triangle or square or polygon. ― -b10- And (assumed tropical:) A square root; called in arithmetic ja*orN : see $aYo'N , near the end of the paragraph.] ― -b11- One says also, humo EalaY~a DilaEN jaAy^irapN , (S, A, O, K, in the last of which, between hm and ElY~ is inserted ka*aA ,) and ↓ DiloEN is allowable, (S, TA,) meaning (tropical:) They are assembled against me with hostility: (A, TA:) the origin of which is the saying of AZ, one says, humo EalaY~N A_ilobN waAHidN [or A^alobN waAHidN ] and SadoEN waAHidN and DilaEN waAHidN , meaning as above. (TA.)

Ehn .) ― -b6- And (assumed tropical:) A line that is made on the ground, after which another line is made, and then the space between these two is sown. (TA.) ― -b7- And (assumed tropical:) A small mountain apart from others: (S, O, K:) or a small mountain, such as is not long: (TA:) or a low and narrow mountain, (Aboo-Nasr, S, O, K, TA,) long and extended: or, accord. to As, a small mountain, extending lengthwise upon the earth, not high. (TA.)

definition: is from AlD~alaAEapu [inf.
sourceDefinition: is from AlD~alaAEapu [inf. n. of DaluEa ]: so in the saying, fulaAnN muDoTaliEN bih`*aA AlA^amori i. e. Such a one is possessed of strength, or power, sufficient for this affair: so says ISk: and he adds that one should not say muT~aliEN : Aboo-Nasr Ahmad Ibn- Hátim says, one says huwa muDoTaliEN bih`*aA AlA^amori and muT~aliEN lh [also]; AlAiDoTilaAEu being from AlD~alaAEapu meaning Alquw~apu ; and AlAiT~ilaAEu being from AlEuluw~u , from the saying AiT~alaEotu Alv~aniy~apa meaning EalawotuhaA [I ascended upon the mountain, or mountain-road, termed vaniy~ap ]; i. e. he is one who has ascendancy with respect to this affair, who is master of it: (S, O, TA:) Lth expressly allows muT~aliEN for muDoTaliEN by the incorporation of the D into the [letter that is originally] t , so that the two together become T with teshdeed. (TA.) And lih`*aA AlA^amori ↓ huwa muDoliEN means the same as muDoTaliEN as first expl. above, i. e. He is possessed of strength, or power, sufficient for this affair. (O, K. [In both, in this instance, lih`*aA , not bih`*aA .]) In the phrase A_i*aA kaAna muDoTaliEFA EalaY Haq~ihi [ If he be possessed of power, or ability, to obtain his right, or due ], it seems that mDTlEA is made trans. by means of ElY because made to imply the meaning of qaAdirFA or muqotadirFA . (Mgh.) ↓ musotaDoliEN , likewise, signifies Having strength, or power. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. yaToHuw , inf. n. TaHowN ; and TaHaY , aor. yaToHaY , inf. n. TaHoYN ; two dial. vars., though only TaHaY , like saEaY , is mentioned in the K; (TA;) He spread [a thing]; spread [it] out, or forth; expanded [it] ; or extended [it]. (K, TA.) You say, TaHawotuhu , like daHawotuhu , i. e. I spread it; &c. (S.) ― -b2- And you say, Alqawomu yaToHaY baEoDuhumo baEoDFA The people, or party, repel one another. (TA.) -A2- TaHaY , (K,) or TaHaA , (TA,) also signifies It, or he, became spread, spread out or forth, expanded, or extended; (K, TA;) being intrans. as well as trans. (TA.) Accord. to As, (TA,) TaHaA mina AlD~arobapi means He became extended (S, TA) upon the ground (TA) in consequence of the blow: (S, TA:) [and this is probably meant by what here follows:] TaHaA is said when one throws down a man upon his face; (K, TA;) or when he spreads, or extends, him; or when he prostrates him on the ground: (TA:) but accord. to Fr, one says, ↓ $ariba Hat~aY TaH~aY i. e. [ He drank until ] he stretched out his legs: and AlbaEiyru ↓ TH~Y A_ilaY AlA^aroDi i. e. The camel stuck to the ground, either from emptiness or from emaciation: and in like manner one says of a man when people call him to aid or to do an act of kindness: the verb being in all these instances with teshdeed: as though, by saying this, he contradicted As as to its being without teshdeed. (TA.) Accord. to AA, (S,) TaHayotu means I lay, or lay upon my side, or laid my side upon the ground. (S, K. *) And you say, ↓ naAma fulaAnN fataTaH~aY i. e. [ Such a one slept, and ] lay, or lay upon his side, in a wide space of ground. (TA.) ― -b2- Also, i. e. TaHaA , (AA, S,) or TaHaY , (K,) He (a man, AA, S) went away into the country, or in the land: (AA, S, K:) like TahaA . (S in art. Thw .) One says, maA A^adoriY A^ayona TaHaA [ I know not whither he has gone away &c.]. (S.) And TaHaA bihi qalobuhu His heart carried him away ( *ahaba bihi ) in [the pursuit of] anything: (S, K:) whence the saying of Alkameh Ibn-'Abadeh, TaHaA bika qalobN fiY AlHisaAni Taruwbu buEayoda Al$~abaAbi EaSora HaAna ma$iybu [ A heart much affected with emotion has carried thee away in the pursuit of the beauties long after youthfulness, in the time when entering upon hoariness has arrived: buEayoda being here a dim. used for the purpose of enhancement]. (S, TA.) And TaHaY bika ham~aka Thy anxiety has carried thee away in a far-extending course. (TA.) And TaHaY biAlkurapi He threw the ball. (TA.) And TaHaY bifulaAnK $aHomuhu Such a one became fat. (TA.) ― -b3- TaHaA , aor. yaToHuw , signifies also He, or it, was or became, distant, or remote. (K.)

definition: , aor. , inf. n. TarofN , He looked from the outer angle of the eye: or [ he twinkled with his eye, i. e.] he put the edge of his eyelid in motion, or in a state of commotion, and looked: (M, TA:) or...
sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. TarofN , He looked from the outer angle of the eye: or [ he twinkled with his eye, i. e.] he put the edge of his eyelid in motion, or in a state of commotion, and looked: (M, TA:) or AlT~arofu signifies the putting the eyelids in motion, or in a state of commotion, in looking: (Mgh, * TA:) one says, $axaSa baSaruhu famaA yaTorifu [ His eye, or eyes, has, or have, become fixedly open, or raised, and he does not put his eyelids in motion, or does not twinkle with his eye, or eyes, in looking ]: (TA:) [or] one says, Tarafa AlbaSaru , aor. and inf. n. as above, meaning the eye, or eyes, [ twinkled, or] became in a state of commotion: (Msb:) [or] Tarafa baSarahu , (O, K, TA, and so in a copy of the S,) or baSaruhu , (so in one of my copies of the S,) aor. and inf. n. as above, [ he winked, i. e.] he closed one of his eyelids upon the other: (S, O, K: [see also 4:]) or Tarafa biEayonihi [in the CK bEayonayohi ] he put his eyelids in motion, or in a state of commotion: (K, TA:) and Turifato Eayonuhu , aor. tuTorafu , inf. n. as above, his eyelids were put in motion or in a state of commotion, by looking. (As, TA.) [Another meaning of Tarafa baSarahu , and another of Turifato said of the eye, will be found below.] EayonN taTorifu , signifying An eye that [ twinkles, or] puts the eyelid in motion, or in a state of commotion, with looking, is used for *uw EayonK taTorifu , meaning (assumed tropical:) a living being. (Mgh.) maA baqiyato minohumo EayonN taTorifu [ There remained not of them one having an eye twinkling ] means (tropical:) they died, (O, K, TA,) or (O, in the K erroneously “ and, ” TA) they were slain. (O, K, TA.) ― -b2- [Also He looked: for] AlT~arofu is used as meaning the act of looking (Er-Rághib, Msb, TA) because the putting in motion of the eyelid constantly attends that act: (Er-Rághib, TA:) and Tarafotuhu , inf. n. as above, signifies I saw, or I looked at or towards, him, or it; syn. A^aboSarotuhu . (Ham p. 111.) It is said in the Kur [xiv. 44] laA yarotad~u A_ilayohimo Tarofuhumo [ Their look shall not revert to them; i. e., shall not be withdrawn by them from that upon which they shall look]. (S, O.) And in the same [xxvii. 40], A^anaA A=tiyka bihi qabola A^ano yarotadN A_ilayoka Tarofuka , [meaning, in like manner, I will bring it to thee before thy look at a thing shall revert to thee, or be withdrawn by thee therefrom: or,] accord. to Fr, meaning before a thing shall be brought to thee from the extent of thy vision: or, as some say, in the space in which thou shalt open thine eye and then close it: or in the space in which one shall reach the extent of thy vision. (O.) And one says, naZara fulaAnN biTarofK xafiY~K [ Such a one looked with a furtive glance ], meaning, contracted his eyelids over the main portion of his eye and looked with the rest of it, by reason of shyness or fear. (Har p. 565.) And taTorifu Alr~ijaAla [app. meaning She looks at the men ] is said of a woman who does not keep constantly to one. (TA. [See maToruwfapN .]) And taTorifu Alr~iyaADa rawoDapF baEoda rawoDapK [app. meaning She looks at the meadows, meadow after meadow, to pasture upon them in succession,] is said of a she-camel such as is termed TarifapN [q. v.]. (As, TA.) ― -b3- Tarafotu Eayonahu , (S, O, Msb, in the K Tarafa Eayonahu ,) aor. and inf. n. as above, (Msb, TA,) I (S, O, Msb) hit, struck, smote, or hurt, his eye with a thing, (S, O, Msb, K, [in the CK $aYo'N is put for bi$aYo'K ,]) such as a garment or some other thing, (TA,) so that it shed tears: and one says of the eye, Turifato . (S, O, K. [See another explanation of the latter in the first sentence.]) Ziyád, in reciting a xuTobap , said, qado Tarafato A^aEoyunakumu Ald~unoyaA wasad~ato masaAmiEakumu Al$~ahawaAtu [ The good of the present world hath smitten your eyes, and appetences have stopped your ears ]. (O.) And one says Tarafahu and ↓ Tr~fhu meaning He, or it, struck, smote, or hurt, his eye. (TA.) And TarafahaA AlHuzonu waAlbukaA='u Grief and weeping hurt it (the eye), so that it shed tears. (TA.) And TarafahaA Hub~u Alr~ijaAli The love of the men smote her eye, so that she raised her eyes and looked at every one that looked at her; as though a Tarofap [or red spot of blood], or a stick or the like, hurt her eye. (Az, TA.) ― -b4- AlT~arofu signifies also The slapping with the hand (K, TA) upon the extremity of the eye. (TA.) ― -b5- Then it became applied to signify The striking upon the head. (TA.) ― -b6- Tarafahu Eanohu signifies He turned him, or it, away, or back, from him, or it. (S, O, K.) Hence the saying of a poet, (S, O, TA,) 'Amr Ibn-Abee-Rabee'ah, (TA,) or a young woman of the Ansár, (O,) A_in~aka waA@ll~`hi la*uw mal~apK yaTorifuka AlA^adonaY Eani AlA^aboEadi so in the S; but the right reading is Eani AlA^aqodami , for the next verse ends with taSorimiY : (IB, TA:) [i. e. Verily thou, by Alláh, art one having a weariness: the nearer turns thee away, or back, from the older: ] meaning, he turns away, or back, thy sight from the latter: i. e. thou takest the new ( Aljadiyda ↓ tasotaTorifu ), and forgettest the old. (S, TA.) You say, Tarafotu AlbaSara Eanohu (S * Msb) I turned away, or back, the sight from him, or it. (Msb.) And AiTorifN baSaraka Turn away, or back, thy sight from that upon which it has fallen and to which it has been extended. (TA.) ― -b7- And Tarafahu Ean~aA $ugolN Business, or occupation, withheld him from us. (TA.) ― -b8- And Tarafahu He drove him away. (Sh, TA.) -A2- Tarifato , (S, O, K,) [aor. ,] inf. n. TarafN ; (TA;) and ↓ tTr~ft ; She (a camel) depastured the sides, or lateral parts, ( A^aToraAf ,) of the pasturage, not mixing with the other she-camels, (S, O, K,) tasting, and not keeping constantly to one pasturage. (Har p. 569.) -A3- Tarufa , (S, O, Msb, K,) inf. n. TaraAfapN , (O, TA,) It (property) was recently, or newly, acquired: (S, O, K: *) or it (a thing) was good [ and recent or new or fresh ]. (Msb.) ― -b2- And the same verb, (S, K,) inf. n. as above, (S, TA,) He was such as is termed TariyfN [and TarifN q. v.] as meaning the contr. of quEodud . (S, K.)

(O.) And one says Tarafahu and ↓ Tr~fhu meaning He, or it, struck, smote, or hurt, his eye. (TA.) And TarafahaA AlHuzonu waAlbukaA='u Grief and weeping hurt it (the eye), so that it shed tears. (TA.) And TarafahaA Hub~u Alr~ijaAli The love of the men smote her eye, so that she raised her eyes and looked at every one that looked at her; as though a Tarofap [or red spot of blood], or a stick or the like, hurt her eye. (Az, TA.) ― -b4- AlT~arofu signifies also The slapping with the hand (K, TA) upon the extremity of the eye. (TA.) ― -b5- Then it became applied to signify The striking upon the head. (TA.) ― -b6- Tarafahu Eanohu signifies He turned him, or it, away, or back, from him, or it. (S, O, K.) Hence the saying of a poet, (S, O, TA,) 'Amr Ibn-Abee-Rabee'ah, (TA,) or a young woman of the Ansár, (O,) A_in~aka waA@ll~`hi la*uw mal~apK yaTorifuka AlA^adonaY Eani AlA^aboEadi so in the S; but the right reading is Eani AlA^aqodami , for the next verse ends with taSorimiY : (IB, TA:) [i. e. Verily thou, by Alláh, art one having a weariness: the nearer turns thee away, or back, from the older: ] meaning, he turns away, or back, thy sight from the latter: i. e. thou takest the new ( Aljadiyda ↓ tasotaTorifu ), and forgettest the old. definition: The eye; a word having no pl. in this sense because it is originally an inf. n., (S, O, K,) therefore it may denote a sing. and may also denote a pl. number [i. e. may signify also eyes ]: (S, O,...
sourceDefinition: The eye; a word having no pl. in this sense because it is originally an inf. n., (S, O, K,) therefore it may denote a sing. and may also denote a pl. number [i. e. may signify also eyes ]: (S, O, Msb:) or, (K,) as Ibn-'Abbád says, (O,) it is a coll. n. signifying the baSar [which has the sing. and the pl. meanings mentioned above, as well as the meaning of the sense of sight ], and is not dualized nor pluralized: or, as some say, it has for pl. A^aToraAfN : (O, K:) but this is refuted by the occurrence of Tarof in a pl. sense in the Kur xxxvii. 47 and xxxviii. 52 and lv. 56: (O:) and though AlA^aToraAf is said to occur as its pl. in a trad. of Umm-Selemeh, this is a mistake for AlA_iToraAq : (Z, O:) it is said, however, that its being originally an inf. n. is not a reason for its not being allowable to pluralize it when it has become a subst., and especially when it is not meant to convey the signification of an epithet: (MF:) [but it may be regarded as an epithet; meaning seer, and, being originally an inf. n., seers also; and this is the more probable because] ↓ AlT~awaArifu [is an epithet used as a subst., and thus] signifies the eyes, (S, O, K,) as in the saying huwa bimakaAnK laA taraAhu AlT~awaArifu [ He is in a place in which the eyes will not see him ]; (S, * O, * TA;) pl. of ↓ TaArifapN . (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] AlT~arofu is the name of (assumed tropical:) Two stars, which precede Aljabohapu , (S, O, K,) so called because (K) they are [regarded as] the two eyes of Leo; one of the Mansions of the Moon: (S, O, K:) [often called AlT~arofapu , q. v.:] the Tarof of Leo, consisting of two small stars in front of Aljabohap , like the faroqadaAni , but inferior to them in light, and having somewhat of obliquity; the Ninth Mansion of the Moon: (Kzw in his descr. of that Mansion:) or the star [app. lambda] in the face of Leo, together with that which is outside [app. alpha] on the figure of Cancer: (Kzw in his descr. of Leo:) or the bright star [alpha] on the hinder, southern, leg, or foot, [i. e. claw, ] of Cancer. (Kzw in his descr. of Cancer.) [See manaAzilu Alqamari , in art. nzl .] ― -b3- And Tarofu AlEayoni signifies The eyelid. definition: The extremity, or end, of anything;
sourceDefinition: The extremity, or end, of anything; [as of a sword, and of a spear, and of a rope, and of the tongue, &c.;] thus accord. to ISd; but in the K this meaning is assigned to ↓ TarofN : (TA: [several evidences of the correctness of the former word in this sense will be found in the present art.; and countless instances of it occur in other arts. &c.: it seems to have been generally regarded by the lexicographers as too notorious to need its being mentioned:]) and a side; a lateral, or an outward, or adjacent, part or portion; a region, district, quarter, or tract; syn. naAHiyapN : (S, O, Msb, K:) and a part, portion, piece, or bit, (syn. TaAy^ifapN ,) of a thing: (S, O, K:) it is used in relation to bodies, or material things, and to times &c.; (Er-Rághib, TA;) and is thus used in the sense of TaAy^ifap of a people, in the Kur iii. 122; (Ksh;) [and may often be rendered somewhat of a thing, whether material (as land &c.) or not material (as in the T and S voce *arowN , where it is used of a saying, and as in the S and A and K in art. hws &c., where it is used of madness, or insanity, or diabolical possession):] the pl. is A^aToraAfN . (O, Msb, K.) ― -b2- [Hence,] AlA^aToraAfu signifies The fingers: and [when relating to the fingers] has no sing. unless this is used as a prefixed noun, as in the saying A^a$aArato biTarafi A_iSobaEihaA [ She made a sign with the end of her finger ]: but the pl. is said by Az to be used in the sense of the sing. in the following ex. cited by Fr, yubodiyna A^aToraAfFA liTaAfFA EanayahN [so that the meaning is, They show an elegant finger like a fruit of the species of tree called Eanam ]; therefore the poet says Eamanah [which is a n. un.: but I think that it is much more reasonable, and especially as the verb is pl., to regard the h in this case as the h of pausation, of which see an ex. voce HiynN ; and accordingly to render the saying, they show elegant fingers like fruits of the Eanam ]. (TA.) It is said in a trad. of Abraham, when he was a little child, juEila rizoquhu fiY A^aToraAfihi [ His sustenance was made to be in his fingers ]; meaning that he used to suck his fingers and find in them that which nourished him. (TA.) ― -b3- And [hence] A^aToraAfu AlEa*aAraY (tropical:) A species of grapes, (A, K, TA,) white and slender, found at Et-Táïf: (A, TA:) or, as in the L, black and long, resembling acorns, likened to the fingers of virgins, that are dyed [ with Hin~aA=' ], because of their length; and the bunch of which is about a cubit long. (TA.) ― -b4- *uw AlT~arafayoni is an appellation of A sort of serpent, (K,) a sort of black serpent, (TA,) or the [ serpent called ] A^asowad , (O,) having two stings, one in its nose and the other in its tail, with both of which, (O, K, TA,) so it is said, (O, TA,) it smites, and it suffers not him whom it smites to linger, killing at once. (O, K, TA.) ― -b5- TarafaA Ald~aAb~api sometimes means The fore part and the hinder part of the beast. (TA.) ― -b6- And A^aToraAfu Aljasadi (O) or Albadani (K) means [ The extremities of the body; i. e.] the arms or hands, and the legs or feet, and the head: (O, K:) or, as in the L, A^aToraAfN is pl. of TarafN as syn. with $awaApN [n. un. of $awFY , q. v.]. (TA.) ― -b7- [And the dual has various other meanings assigned to it, derived from the first of the significations mentioned in this paragraph.] It is said in a trad. (O, K) of the Prophet, (O,) kaAna A_i*aA A@$otakaY A^aHadN mino A^aholihi lamo tazali Alburomapu EalaY Aln~aAri Hat~aY yaA^otiYa EalaY A^aHadi Tarafayohi [ It was the case that when any one of his family had a complaint, the cooking-pot did not cease to be on the fire but he arrived at one of his two limits ]; meaning (assumed tropical:) convalescence or death; because these are the two terminations of the case of the diseased. (O, K.) ― -b8- And one says, laA yamoliku Tarafayohi (assumed tropical:) He will not have control over his mouth and his anus: referring to him who has drunk medicine or become intoxicated. (AO, ISk, S, O, K.) ― -b9- And fulaAnN faAsidu AlT~arafiyoni (assumed tropical:) Such a one is corrupt in respect of the tongue and the faroj . (TA.) ― -b10- And laA yadoriY A^aY~u Tarafayohi A^aTowalu , (in the CK yudoraY ,) [ He will not, or does not, know which of his two extremities is the longer, ] meaning (tropical:) his *akar and his tongue; (S, O, K, TA;) whence TarafN is used as signifying (assumed tropical:) the tongue: (TA:) or the meaning is, as some say, (assumed tropical:) which of his two halves is the longer; the lower or the upper: (TA:) or (assumed tropical:) the lineage of his father or that of his mother (O, K, TA) in respect of generosity, or nobility: (O, TA:) i. e., which of his two parents is the more generous, or noble: so says Fr. (TA.) ― -b11- kariymu AlT~arafayoni means (tropical:) Generous, or noble, [ on both sides, i. e.] in respect of male and female ancestors. (S, O, TA.) ― -b12- And A^aToraAfN means also (assumed tropical:) A man's father and mother and brothers and paternal uncles and any relations whom it is unlawful for him to marry. (AZ, S, O, K.) ― -b13- And (assumed tropical:) Noble, or exalted, men: (Th, S:) or A^aToraAfu AlA^aroDi means (tropical:) the noble, or exalted, men, and the learned men, of the earth, or land: (O, K, TA:) one of whom is termed TarafN , or ↓ TirofN . (O, See the latter of these words.) And hence, as some explain it, the saying in the Kur [xiii. 41, like one in xxi. 45], A^awalamo yarawoA A^an~aA naA^otiY A@loA^aroDa nanoquSuhaA mino A^aToraAfihaA (assumed tropical:) [ Have they not seen that we visit, or bring destruction upon, the land, curtailing it of its learned men? ]; the meaning being, the death of its learned men: (O, TA:) or, as some say, [ curtailing it of its inhabitants and its fruits; for they say that] the meaning is, the death of its inhabitants and the diminution of its fruits: (TA:) or it means, curtailing it of its sides, or districts, one by one: (Az, O, L:) Ibn-'Arafeh says that the meaning is, we lay open by conquest, to the Prophet, ( nafotaHu EalaY Aln~abiY~i ,) the country around Mekkeh. (O, TA.) [― -b14- A^aToraAfu Aln~aAsi also means (assumed tropical:) The lower orders of the people: but this I believe to be post-classical.] ― -b15- TarafaYi Aln~ahaAri , in the Kur xi. 116, means gudowapF waEa$iy~apF [i. e. Morning and afternoon ]; by the former being meant daybreak; and by the latter, noon and the EaSor [q. v.], (Ksh, Bd,) or the EaSor [only]. (Bd.) And A^aToraAfa Aln~ahaAri , in the Kur xx. 130, means At daybreak and at sunset: (Ksh, Bd:) or at noon and at the EaSor ; so says Zj: or, accord. to IAar, in the hours ( saAEaAt ) of the day: Abu-l-'Abbás says that it means TarafaYi Aln~ahaAri . (TA.) ― -b16- [ EalaY TarafK often occurs as meaning Beside, aside, or apart; like ElY jaAnibK , and ElY naAHiyapK : and in like manner the Persians say baro Tarafo . ― -b17- And mino Tarafi fulaAnK is often used as meaning On the part of such a one; but is perhaps post-classical.] ― -b18- And you say, liloA^amori TarafaAni [meaning (assumed tropical:) There are two ways of performing the affair, either of which may be chosen; as though it had two ends, or two sides]. (TA voce SaroEN .) And jaEalahu muTolaqa AlT~arafayoni (assumed tropical:) [ He made it allowable, or free, in respect of both the alternatives, either way one might choose to take ]. (Msb in art. bwH .) ― -b19- [And hence, perhaps,] TarafN signifies also (assumed tropical:) Anything chosen or choice: pl. A^aToraAfN : [whence] A^aToraAfu AlHadiyvi means (assumed tropical:) Chosen, or choice, subjects of discourse; as also AlHadiyvi ↓ TaraAy^ifu : and A^aToraAfu AlA^aHaAdiyvi means [the same, or] colloquies of friends, consisting of mutual communications, and oblique expressions, and allusions: so says ISd: and this is likewise a meaning of ↓ AlT~iraAfu and Als~ibaAbu , which latter [properly signifying “ mutual reviling ”] is given in the K as an explanation of the former. (TA.) ― -b20- Also Flesh, or flesh-meat; syn. laHomN . (TA.)

(O, TA.) (TA.) ― -b20- Also Flesh, or flesh-meat; syn. laHomN . (TA.)

sourceDefinition: [ A wink, i. e.] a closing of one of the eyelids upon the other: (S, O, K:) or [ a twinkling of the eye, i. e.] a putting the eyelids in motion or in a state of commotion. (K.) One says A^asoraEu mino Tarofapi EayonK [ Quicker than a wink, or a twinkling of an eye ]. (S, O.) And maA yufaAriquniY Tarofapa EayonK [ He does not separate himself from me during a wink, or a twinkling of an eye ]. (TA.) ― -b2- Also A red spot of blood, in the eye, occasioned by a blow or some other cause. (S, O, K.) ― -b3- And A brand, or mark made with a hot iron, having to it no A^aToraAf [or sides, or lateral portions ], being only a line. (Ibn-'Abbád, O, K.) -A2- And AlT~arofapu A certain star or asterism ( najomN ). (K. [There thus mentioned as though different from the asterism commonly called AlT~arofu , which I do not believe to be the case: see the latter appellation.])

sourceDefinition: [pass. part. n. of Tarafa , q. v.]. You say, fulaAnN maToruwfu AlEayoni bifulaAnK , meaning Such a one is, exclusively of others, looked at by such a one. (S, O.) ― -b2- And EayonN maToruwfapN An eye of which the lids are put in motion or in a state of commotion, by looking. (As, TA.) [And] An eye, hit, struck, smitten, or hurt, with a thing, so that it sheds tears. (S, O, K.) And ↓ TariyfN applied to an eye signifies the same as maToruwfapN [in one of these senses, but in which of them is not said]. (TA.) ― -b3- maToruwfapN applied to a woman means As though her eye were hit, struck, smitten, or hurt, with something, (O, and EM p. 83,) so that it shed tears, (O,) by reason of the languish of her look; (EM ibid;) and this is said to be its meaning in the saying of Tarafeh, A_i*aA naHonu qulonaA A^asomiEiynaA A@nobarato lanaA EalaY risolihaA maToruwfapF lamo ta$ad~ad (O, EM,) i. e. When we say, “ Sing thou to us, ” she betakes herself to us in her gentle way, as though her eye were hurt by something, by reason of the languish of her look, not straining herself in her singing; but as some relate the verse, the word is maToruwqapF , meaning “ weakly: ” (EM:) or it means whose eye the love of men has smitten, so that she raises her eyes and looks at every one that looks at her; as though a Tarofap [or red spot of blood], or a stick or the like, hurt her eye: (Az, TA:) or having a languishing eye; as though it were turned away, or back, ( TurifatN ,) from everything at which it looked: (IAar, TA:) or as though her eye were turned away, or back so that it, or she, is still: (TA:) or (assumed tropical:) who looks at the men ( taTorifu Alr~ijaAla ); i. e. (assumed tropical:) who does not keep constantly to one; the pass. part. n. being put in the place of the act.; but Az says that this explanation is at variance with the original purport of the word: (TA:) or maToruwfapN biAlr~ijaAl means (tropical:) a woman who raises, or stretches and raises, her eye at men, (S, O, K, TA,) and turns away her look from her husband, to others, (S, TA, *) and in whom is no good: (TA:) or (assumed tropical:) who looks not at any but the men; (K;) or maToruwfapu AlEayoni biAlr~ijaAli has this meaning. (AA, TA.) -A2- A^aroDN maToruwfapN Land abounding with the herbage called Tariyfap . (S, O, K.)

definition: , (S, TA,) or Tw~qhu TawoqFA , (O, K, TA,) inf.
sourceDefinition: , (S, TA,) or Tw~qhu TawoqFA , (O, K, TA,) inf. n. taTowiyqN , (TA,) He attired him with a Tawoq [or neck-ring ]. (S, TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] Taw~aqotuhu Al$~aYo'a means (assumed tropical:) I made the thing to be [ as though it were ] his Tawoq [or neck-ring ]: and thereby is expressed the imposing [upon one] a thing that is difficult, troublesome, or inconvenient: (Msb:) [i. e.] Taw~aqotuka Al$~aYo'a means (assumed tropical:) I imposed, or have imposed, upon thee the thing as one that is difficult, troublesome, or inconvenient. (S, O, K. *) sayuTaw~aquwna maA baxiluwA bihi , in the Kur [iii. 176], means (assumed tropical:) They shall have that whereof they were niggardly made to cleave to their necks [ like the neck-ring ]: (O, TA:) as is said in a trad., it shall be made a biting snake upon the neck. (Jel.) And [in the Kur ii. 180] some read, waEalaY A@l~a*iyna yuTaw~aquwnahu , [in the CK, erroneously, yuTaw~iquwnahu ,] meaning, (assumed tropical:) And upon those who shall have it put [ upon them ] like the Tawoq upon their necks [ shall be incumbent &c.]: (K, TA:) which is like the saying yuja$~amuwnahu and yukal~afuwnahu [i. e. shall have it imposed upon them as a thing that is difficult, troublesome, or inconvenient ]: (TA:) another reading is ↓ yaT~aw~aquwnahu , [in the CK, erroneously, yuT~aw~aquwnahu ,] originally yataTaw~aquwnahu [meaning the same as the former reading]: and another, ↓ yuTay~aquwnahu , originally yuTayowaquwnahu [also meaning the same; in the CK, erroneously, yuTayoquwnahu ]: and another, ↓ yaT~ay~aquwnahu , [in the CK, erroneously, with damm to the first letter, and so in what follows,] originally yataTayowaquwnahu [also meaning the same]. (TA.) ― -b2- Taw~aqato lahu nafosuhu (Akh, S, O, K) is syn. with Taw~aEato , (Akh, S, O,) meaning His soul, or mind, facilitated to him [the doing of a thing]. (Akh, S, O, K.)

definition: A curved construction or structure;
sourceDefinition: A curved construction or structure; (S, O, K;) [said to be] a Pers. word arabicized; (S, O;) and its pl. is TaAqaAtN and TiyqaAnN : (S, O, K:) or an arch of a building, wherever it is; and the pl. is A^aTowaAqN and TiyqaAnN : (JK, TA:) and as signifying [thus, or] an arch constructed with bricks, it is [said to be] originally ↓ TaAy^iqN ; and therefore to have for its pl. TawaAy^iqu : so says Az. (TA.) [It is often applied to An arched gateway or doorway: and to a vault. And] i. q. kuw~apN [i. e. A mural aperture; a hole, or an aperture, in a wall; a meaning also assigned to A_iforiyzN , by which TaAqN will be found to be expl. in what follows: or a niche in a wall; which, as also a window, is now often called ↓ TaAqapN ]. (So in the Munjid of Kr.) [And app. A kind of arched construction with a flat top which forms a shelf, against a wall. (See raf~N and sahowapN .)] And i. q. A_iforiyzN [which is expl. as meaning a projecting roof or covering of a wall: and a projecting coping, or ledge, or cornice, surrounding the upper part of a wall: and in the KL as meaning a hole, or an aperture, of a wall; (as mentioned above;) but its author adds “ so we have heard ”]: (MA voce A_iforiyzN :) or so A^aTowaAqN . (JK, and O on the authority of Ibn-'Abbád. [But this I think doubtful, and the more so as it will be seen in what follows that another meaning assigned in these same lexicons to A^aTowaAqN is said by IB to be a meaning of TaAqN .]) ― -b2- See also TaAy^iqN , in two places. ― -b3- [Also A layer, stratum, lamina, or the like; or any flat piece, or portion, of a thing, such as is in some cases placed over, or under, a similar piece or portion: and anything such as is in some cases lined, or faced, or otherwise combined, with another similar thing: pl. TaAqaAtN .] You say TaAqu naEolK [ A single piece of leather of a sole that consists of two or more of such pieces]; (S, O, K;) and nEolK ↓ TaAqapu [which means the same]. (K.) And naEolN TaAqN waAHidN A single sole; i. e. a sole of a single piece; not made of two pieces sewed together, one upon the other. (TA in art. nEl .) And [in like manner] a garment is said to be TaAqN waAHidN [i. e. Single, not double, not lined nor faced nor stuffed ]. (Az, in TA in art. smT , [where this meaning is clearly indicated,] and Th, in M, same art.) Thus one says saraAwiylu TaAqN waAHidN [ Trousers, or drawers, of single cloth ]. (Th, M and K in art. smT .) [See also what is said of the phrase Als~araAwiylu AlT~aAqu voce rijolN .] One says also gazolN TaAqN waAHidN [ Spun thread that is a single yarn ]: and gazolN mafotuwlN TaAqayoni [ Spun thread twisted of two yarns ]. (S and TA in art. sHl .) See also TaAqapN , which has a similar meaning. [And see an ex. of the pl. TaAqaAt voce raboEapN .] -A2- Also A certain sort of garment, (S, O, K,) having sleeves. (S, O.) [And] accord. to Esh-Shereeshee, A garment worn by a new-born child, or young infant, without an opening at the bosom. (Har p. 502.) ― -b2- And (O, K) accord. to IAar, (O,) A [ garment of the kind called ] TayolasaAn [q. v.]: (O, K:) or such as is A^axoDar [properly meaning green; but when applied to a garment commonly meaning, as used by the Arabs, of a dark, or an ashy, dust-colour; or a dingy ashcolour ]: (Kr, K:) pl. TiyqaAnN , like siyjaAnN pl. of saAjN . (TA.) ― -b3- And A [ garment of the kind called ] kisaA='i : (IB, TA:) and (TA) so A^aTowaAqN . (JK, and O and TA on the authority of Ibn- 'Abbád. [But this, as I have shown above, I think doubtful.]) ― -b4- And A [ woman's muffler, or head-covering, such as is called ] ximaAr . (IAar, TA.) ― -b5- And one says, raA^ayotu A^aroDFA kaA^an~ahaA AlT~iyqaAnu (tropical:) [ I saw a land as though it were spread with the garments called TyqAn ]; meaning, whereof the herbage was abundant. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: is the subst. from A^aTaAqa , (Az, Msb, K,) and is used in the place of the inf. n., (Az, TA,) and [when used as a simple subst.] signifies Ability, or power; (S, O, * Msb, K;) and so ↓ TawoqN , (S, O, K,) which is [originally] an inf. n., (Az, K,) and is also expl. as meaning the utmost that one can do, with difficulty, trouble, or inconvenience. (TA.) One says, [ laA TaAqapa liY bihi I have not ability, or power, to do it, or to bear or endure or tolerate it: and, to cope with him: (see Kur ii. last verse: and verse 250:) and] ↓ huwa fiY TawoqiY It is within my ability, or power. (S.) In the phrase Talabotahu TaAqataka , [as meaning Thou soughtest him, or it, in thy state of ability, or power, ] Sb says, the [quasi-] inf. n. is prefixed [to the pronoun, and thus rendered determinate], though occupying the place of a denotative of state; in like manner as the article Al is prefixed [to ErAk ] in the phrase A^arosalahaA . (TA.) -A2- [Also A slender and small bundle or fascicle of fibres or filaments or the like, one of those whereof two or more, twisted together, compose a rope; a strand, a yarn, a single twist, or single thread, of a rope or cord or fringe &c.] You say TaAqapN mino HabolK A strand, yarn, or single twist, of a rope; syn. quw~apN ; (S voce quw~apN ;) and so mino HabolK ↓ TaAqN , pl. A^aTowaAqN : (JK voce quw~apN :) [the pl. of TaAqapN in this sense is TaAqaAtN :] TaAqaAtu AlHaboli means quwaAhu , as is said in the A. (TA.) ― -b2- And A $uEobap [i. e. spring, spray, bunch, or branchlet, ] of sweet basil, or of sweet-smelling plants: and likewise [ a lock, or flock, ] of hair: (JK, TA:) [and so of wool, and the like;] you say TaAqapu rayoHaAnK , (S, O, K, TA,) [or mino rayoHaAnK , &c.,] meaning $uEobapN minohu , as in the A. (TA.) ― -b3- TaAqapu naEolK : see TaAqN , latter half. ― -b4- See also another meaning of TaAqapN voce TaAqN , first quarter.

sourceDefinition: (S, O, K) and ↓ TaAqN (O, K) A prominence [app. meaning a ledge or ridge ] projecting from a mountain: (S, O, K:) and the former, (S,) or the latter, (K,) or each, (O,) also the like thereof in a well; (S, O, K; [in the CK, Aln~iyri is erroneously put for Albiy^ori ;]) i. e., in the wall that surrounds the interior of a well; and its pl. is TawaAy^iqu : (TA:) and between any two pieces of wood [or planks ] of a ship, or boat: (S, O, K:) or TaAy^iqN signifies one of the pieces of wood [or planks ] of the interior of a zaworaq [or skiff ]: accord. to Aboo-'Amr Esh-Sheybánee, it is the middle. or in the middle, of a ship or boat: and accord. to As, a prominence projecting from a ship, or boat, like a ledge swelling out from a mountain: and also, he says, a ridge, or ledge, in a [ mountain, or portion of a mountain, such as is termed ] qun~ap : accord. to Lth, TaAy^iqu kul~i $aYo'K signifies any mountain, or [ hill such as is termed ] A^akamap , that surrounds anything: and its pl. is A^aTowaAqN [like A^aSoHaAbN pl. of SaAHibN ]. (TA.) ― -b2- TaAy^iqN also signifies, accord. to Ibn-Hamzeh, The curved extremity of a bow; which is said to be called its ↓ TaAq ; but this he disallows. (TA.) ― -b3- See also TaAqN , first sentence.

sourceDefinition: , aor. yaZil~u , inf. n. ZilaAlapN : see 4. -A2- Zal~a , (T, M, Msb, K,) first pers. Zalilotu , (T, S, M, O, Msb, K,) [and accord. to SM Zalalotu also, for he says that] the verb is of the class of manaEa as well as of the class of taEiba , (TA,) and Zalotu , (T, S, * M, O, K,) likened to lasotu , (M, K, *) formed by rejecting the former l in Zalilotu , (T, O,) and Zilotu , which is [also] originally Zalilotu , (Sb, T, M, O, K,) formed by transferring to the Z the vowel of the rejected l , (Sb, T, M, O,) anomalously, (Sb, M,) the latter of the dial. of the people of El-Hijáz; (T;) aor. yaZal~u ; (S, * M, O, * Msb, K;) imperative AiZolalo and Zalo (T) [and it is implied in the M voce qar~a that one says also AiZolilo and Zilo , which indicates that the aor. is also yaZil~u , but this requires confirmation, which I have not anywhere found]; inf. n. ZuluwlN (T, S, M, O, Msb, K) and Zal~N (M, K) and Zil~N ; (thus also in a copy of the M; [but this I think doubtful;]) accord. to Lth, (T,) or Kh, (Msb,) [i. e. accord. to the author of the 'Eyn,] is said only of a thing that is done in the day, or daytimes; (T, S, M, O, Msb;) like as baAta , aor. yabiytu , is said only of a thing that is done in the night: (T:) it is an incomplete [i. e. a non-attributive] verb, relating to a time in which is a shade from the sun, from morning to evening, or from sunrise to sunset: (Esh-Shiháb, TA:) one says, Zal~a fulaAnN nahaArahu SaAy^imFA [ Such a one was during his day fasting; or he passed his day fasting ]: (Lth, T:) and Zal~a nahaArahu yafoEalu ka*aA [ He was in, or during, his day doing such a thing; or he passed his day doing such a thing ]: (M, K:) and Zalilotu A^aEomalu ka*aA [ I was in the day or daytime, or I passed the day, doing such a thing; or] I did such a thing in the day or daytime. (S, O, Msb. *) In the saying of 'Antarah, walaqado A^abiytu EalaY AlT~awaY waA^aZal~uhu Hat~aY A^anaAla bihi kariyma AlmaA^okali [app. meaning And verily I pass the night in hunger, and I pass the day in it, that I may attain thereby plentiful eating ], A^aZal~uhu is for A^aZal~u Ealayohi . (S, O.) And accord. to some, (TA,) Zal~a layolahu occurs in poetry; (M, K, TA;) so that one says, Zal~a layolahu yafoEalu ka*aA [ He was in, or during, his night, or he passed his night, doing such a thing ]: but it is said that in this case the verb has the meaning next following. (TA.) ― -b2- And it signifies also He, or it, became; syn. SaAra : (Er-Rághib, TA:) being in this sense likewise an incomplete [i. e. a non-attributive] verb, divested of that meaning of time which it radically denotes; as in the phrase in the Kur [xvi. 60 and xliii. 16], Zal~a wajohuhu musowad~FA [ His face becomes black ]: so says Ibn-Málik: (TA:) or this may mean his face continues all the day black: (Bd in xvi. 60:) and one says also, Zal~a yafoEalu ka*aA meaning He continued doing such a thing: this too is mentioned by Ibn-Málik, and is of the dial. of the people of Syria. (TA.) ― -b3- It is also a complete [i. e. an attributive] verb as meaning He, or it, continued; as is said in the Expos. of the “ Shifè, ” and by Ibn-Málik; and, as Ibn-Málik likewise says, it was, or became, long. (TA.)

definition: , said of a day, It was, (S, O,) or became, (M, K,) shady, or a day having shade: (S, M, O, K:) or it was a day having clouds, or other [ causes of shade ]: (T:) or it was continually shady;
sourceDefinition: , said of a day, It was, (S, O,) or became, (M, K,) shady, or a day having shade: (S, M, O, K:) or it was a day having clouds, or other [ causes of shade ]: (T:) or it was continually shady; as also ↓ Zal~a , aor. yaZil~u , inf. n. ZilaAlapN . (Msb.) ― -b2- And, said of a thing, [ It extended its shade; or] its shade extended; as also ↓ Zl~l . (Msb.) -A2- A^aZal~atoniY Al$~ajarapu [ The tree shaded me, or afforded me shade ]: and in like manner one says of other things than trees. (S, O.) A^aZal~aka said of a building, or of a mountain, or of a cloud, means It protected thee, and cast its shade upon thee. (Mgh.) ― -b2- [Hence,] AZl~hu (assumed tropical:) He took him into his shelter, or protection: (TA:) or he guarded, or protected, him, and placed him within the scope of his might, or power of resistance or defence. And AZl~ [alone] (assumed tropical:) It (a thing) advanced: or approached, or drew near. (Msb.) And i. q. A^a$orafa [app. as meaning (assumed tropical:) He, or it, became within sight, or view ]. (Msb.)

definition: properly signifies Shade;
sourceDefinition: properly signifies Shade; i. e. the light of the sun without the rays: when there is no light, it is ZulomapN , not Zil~N : (S, O:) contr. of DiH~N : (M, K:) or i. q. faYo'N : (K:) so some say: (M:) or so the [common] people say: (IKt, Msb:) or the former is [ shade ] in the morning; and the latter is in the evening: (M, K:) or, accord. to IKt, the former is in the morning and in the evening; but the latter is only after the declining of the sun from the meridian: ISk says that the former is from the rising of the sun to its declining; and the latter, from the declining to the setting: Th says that the Zil~ of a tree &c. is in the morning; and the faYo' , in the evening: (Msb:) Ru-beh says, (M, Msb,) any place, (M,) or any thing, (Msb,) upon which the sun has been and which it has quitted is termed Zil~N and faYo'N ; (M, Msb;) but a thing [or place ] upon which the sun has not been is termed Zil~N [only]; and hence it is said that the sun annuls, or supersedes, the Zil~ , and the faYo' annuls, or supersedes, the sun: (Msb:) AHeyth says, the Zil~ is anything upon which the sun has not come; and the term faYo' is applied only after the declining of the sun; the faYo' being eastwards and the Zil~ being westwards; and the Zil~ being termed Zil~ from the beginning of the day to the declining of the sun; after which it is termed faYo' until the night: (T, TA:) one says the Zil~ of Paradise, but not its faYo' , because the sun will never replace its Zil~ ; but En-Nábighah El-Jaadee has assigned to Paradise faYo' having ZilaAl : (M, TA:) in a verse of Aboo-Sakhr ElHudhalee, Zil~N is made fem. as meaning maniy~ap [i. e. death ]: (Ham p. 161:) the pl. [of mult.] is ZilaAlN (S, M, O, K) and ZuluwlN and [of pauc.] A^aZolaAlN . (M, O, K.) The saying of a rájiz, kaA^an~amaA wajohuka Zil~N mino Hajaro [ As though thy face were a shade of a stone ] is said to mean hardness of face, and shamelessness: or the being black in the face: (T, TA:) for the Arabs say that there is nothing more dense in shade than a stone. (TA.) qado DaHaA Zil~uhu [ His shade, or shadow, has become sun ] is said of the dead. (TA.) mar~a binaA kaA^an~ahu Zil~u *iy^obK [ He passed by us as though he were the shadow of a wolf ] means swiftly, as does a wolf. (M.) AinotaEalato ZilaAlahaA (assumed tropical:) [ They made their shadows to be as though they were sandals to them ] is said of camels or other beasts when it is midday in summer and they have no shadow [but such as is beneath them]: a rájiz says, qado waradato tamo$iY EalaY ZilaAlihaA wa*aAbati Al$~amosu EalaY qilaAlihaA [ They came to the water walking upon their shadows, and the sun was intensely hot upon the tops of their heads and humps ]. (T.) And one says, huwa yatobaEu Zil~a nafosihi (tropical:) [ He follows the shadow of himself; i. e. a thing that he will not overtake; for], as a poet says, the shadow that goes with thee thou wilt not overtake by following: and huwa yubaAriY Zil~a nafosihi (tropical:) [ He strives to outstrip the shadow of himself ], meaning that he walks with a proud and self-conceited gait: so in the A. (TA.) And Ainotaqalotu Eano Zil~iY (tropical:) I left my state, or condition. (TA.) And taraka AlZ~aboYu Zil~ahu : so in the T and S and O: (TA:) but [said to be] correctly, A^atorukuhu taroka AlZ~aboYi Zil~ahu , (K,) or laA^atorukan~ahu , (M, TA,) i. e. [ I will forsake him, or I will assuredly forsake him, as the gazelle forsakes ] the place of its shade: (O, TA:) [each, however, is app. right; and the former is the more agreeable with the following explanations:] a prov., (M,) applied to the man who is wont to take fright and flee; for the gazelle, when it takes fright and flees from a thing, never returns to it: (S, O, K:) by the Zil~ is here meant the covert in which it shades and shelters itself in the vehemence of the heat; then the hunter comes to it and rouses it, and it will not return thither; and one says, taraka AlZ~aboYu Zil~ahu , meaning the place of its shade: it is applied to him who takes fright and flees from a thing, and forsakes it so as not to return to it; and to the case of a man's forsaking his companion. (Meyd.) [ vaqiylu AlZ~il~i as applied to a man, see expl. in art. vql : see also Har p. 250, where it is indicated that it may be rendered One whose shadow, even, is oppressive, and therefore much more so is his person.] In the phrase walaA A@lZ~il~u walaA A@loHaruwru , (M, K) in the Kur [xxxv. 20], Th says, accord. to some, (M,) AlZ~il~u means Paradise; (M, K;) and AlHaruwru , the fire [of Hell]: but he adds, I say that AlZ~il~u is the Zil~ itself [i. e. shade ], and AlHaruwru is the Har~ itself [i. e. heat]: (M: [see also HaruwrN :]) and Er-Rághib says that Zil~N is sometimes assigned to anything; whether it be approved, as in the phrase above mentioned; or disapproved, as in waZil~K mino yaHomuwmK in the Kur [lvi. 42, meaning And shade of smoke, or black smoke ]. (TA.) And AlZ~ilaAlu means ZilaAlu Aljan~api [ The shades of Paradise ]: (Fr, T, O, K, TA:) in some copies of the K, waAlZ~ilaAlu Aljan~apu , which is a mistake: (TA:) [but this requires consideration; for] El-'Abbás Ibn- 'Abd-El-Muttalib says, mino qabolihaA Tibota fiY AlZ~ilaAli wafiY musotawodaEK Hayovu yuxoSafu Alwaraqu [ Before it thou wast good in, or in the shades of, Paradise, and in a depositary in the part where leaves are sewed together to conceal the pudenda ]; (T, O, TA;) i. e. before thy descent to the earth (to which the pronoun in qblhA relates), thou wast good in the loins of Adam when he was in Paradise. (TA.) Aljan~apu taHota ZilaAli Als~uyuwfi [ Paradise is beneath the shades of the swords ] is a trad., meaning that fighting against unbelievers is a way of attaining to Paradise. (Marg. note in a copy of the “ Jámi' es-Sagheer.) mulaAEibu Zil~ihi is an appellation of A certain bird; [see art. lEb ;] and one says mulaAEibaA Zil~ihimaA ; and mulaAEibaAtu Zil~ihin~a : but when you make them indeterminate, you say mulaAEibaAtu A^aZolaAlihin~a . (T, O, K. [But in the TA in art. lEb , it is said that one dualizes and pluralizes both nouns, because the appellation becomes determinate.]) ― -b2- Zil~u All~ayoli means (tropical:) The blackness of the night: (T, S, O, Msb;) metaphorically thus termed; (S;) as in the saying, A^ataAnaA fiY Zil~i All~ayoli [ He came to us in the blackness of the night ]: (S, O:) or it signifies junoHu All~ayoli [app. as meaning the darkness, and confusedness, of the night; see junoHN ]; (M, TA;) or so AlZ~il~u : (K:) or this means the night, (M, K, TA,) itself; (M, TA;) so the astronomers say: (TA:) all the night is Zil~N : and so is all the period from the shining of the dawn to the rising of the sun. (T.) ― -b3- Zil~u Aln~ahaAri is The colour of the day when the sun predominates over it [app. meaning when the light of the sun predominates over that of the early dawn ]. sourceDefinition: A thing that covers, or protects, [or shades, ] one, overhead: accord. to Lth, i. q. ↓ maZal~apN or miZal~apN meaning a thing that shades one from the sun: (T:) see an ex. voce miZal~apN : a covering: and i. q. buroTul~apN : (M, K:) this latter word correctly signifies a miZal~ap for the summer: (TA in art. brTl :) and a thing by which one is protected from the cold and the heat: (M:) anything that protects and shades one, as a building or a mountain or a cloud: (Mgh:) the first portion that shades (AZ, S, K) of a cloud (AZ, S) or of clouds; (K;) accord. to Er-Rághib, mostly said of that which is deemed unwholesome, and which is disliked; whence the use of the word in the Kur vii. 170: (TA:) and what shades one, of trees: (K:) or anything that forms a covering over one, (T, TA,) or shades one: (T:) and [particularly] a thing like the Suf~ap [q. v.], (S, M, O, K,) by which one protects himself from the heat and the cold: (K:) or, accord. to the lawyers, Zul~apu Ald~aAri means the sud~ap [or projecting roof ] over the door of the house: or that of which the beams have one end upon the house and the other end upon the wall of the opposite neighbour: (Mgh:) pl. ZulalN (S, M, O, K) and ZilaAlN . (M, K.) [See also ZalaAlN .] One says also, daAmato Zul~apu AlZ~il~i and AlZ~il~i ↓ ZilaAlapu , meaning That whereby one shades himself, (K, TA,) of trees, or of stones, or of other things, (TA,) [ continued. ] Ea*aAbu yawomi AlZ~ul~api , in the Kur. [xxvi. 189], is said to mean [ The punishment of the day of ] clouds beneath which was a hot wind ( samuwm ): (S, O, K:) or an overshadowing cloud, beneath which they collected themselves together, seeking protection thereby from the heat that came upon them, whereupon it covered them, (T, * K, TA,) and they perished beneath it: (T, TA:) or, accord. to some, i. q. Ea*aAbu yawomi AlS~uf~api . (T: see art. Sf .) And lahumo mino fawoqihimo ZulalN mina A@ln~aAri wamino taHotihimo ZulalN , in the Kur [xxxix. 18], means To them shall be above them coverings of fire, and beneath them coverings to those below them; Hell consisting of stages, one beneath another. (T, TA.) Seditions, or conflicts and factions, are mentioned in a trad. as being like Zulal , by which are meant Mountains, and clouds: and El-Kumeyt likens waves of the sea to Zulal . (TA.) And [the pl.] ZulalN is used as meaning The chambers of a prison. (M, TA.) -A2- See also Zal~apN .

definition: A place having shade: (M, K:) or having constant shade.
sourceDefinition: A place having shade: (M, K:) or having constant shade. (T, S, M, O, K.) And hence Zil~N ZaliylN (M, K) Constant shade: (S:) or extensive shade: (O:) or in this case the latter word denotes intensiveness [meaning dense ]; (M, K, TA;) being like $aAEirN in the phrase $iEorN $aAEirN . (TA.) Zil~FA ZaliylFA in the Kur iv. 60 is said by Er-Rághib to be an allusion to ease and pleasantness of life. (TA.) One says also A^ayokapN ZaliylapN A collection of trees tangled, or luxuriant, or abundant and dense. (TA.) In the saying of Uheyhah Ibn-El-Juláh, describing palm-trees, hiYa AlZ~il~u fiY AlHar~i Haq~a AlZ~ali li waAlmanoZaru AlA^aHosanu AlA^ajomalu The final character of line one and the initial character of line two are unclear. [ISd says] in my opinion, he means Al$~aYo'u AlZ~aliylu Haq~a AlZ~aliyli ; [so that the verse should be rendered They are the shade in the heat, the shady thing, the extremely shady, and the most goodly, the most beautiful, thing at which one looks; (see the phrase h`*aA AlEaAlimu Haq~a AlEaAlimi , voce Haq~N ;)] the inf. n. being put in the place of the subst. (M.) laA ZaliylK in the Kur [lxxvii. 31] means Not profitable as the shade in protecting from the heat. (TA.)

definition: [ More, and most, dense in shade ].
sourceDefinition: [ More, and most, dense in shade ]. The Arabs say, layosa $aYo'N A^aZal~a mino HajarK [ There is not anything more dense in shade than a stone ]. (TA.) ― -b2- And A^aZal~ , [as a subst., i. e. A^aZal~N accord. to a general rule, or, if regarded as originally an epithet, it may be A^aZal~u ,] by poetic license A^aZolal , (S, M, O, K,) signifies The under part, (S, O,) or the concealed part, (M, AHei, K,) of the manosim , (S, M, O, K,) or of the xuf~ , (AHei, TA,) [the former app. here used, as it is said be in other cases, in the same sense as the latter, meaning the foot, ] of the camel; (S, M, O, AHei, K;) so called because of its being concealed: (AHei, TA:) and, (M, K,) in a human being, (M,) AlA^aZal~u signifies baTonu AlA_iSobaEi ; (M, K;) and [ISd says] this is in my opinion the right explanation; but it is said that A^aZal~u AlA_inosaAni signifies buTuwnu A^aSaAbiEihi , which means the portion, of what is next to the fore part [ of the bottom ] of the foot, from the root of the great toe to the root of the little toe, of the human being: (M:) the pl. is Zul~N , which is anomalous, (M, K,) or formed after the manner of the pl. of an epithet: (M:) or AlZ~ul~u fiY AlA_inosaAni means the roots, or bases, ( A^uSuwl ) of what are termed buTuwnu AlA^aSaAbiEi , next to the fore part [ of the bottom ] of the foot. (Ibn-'Abbád, O.) Hence the prov., A_ino yadoma A^aZal~uka faqado naqiba xuf~iY [ If the fore part of the sole of thy foot be bleeding, the sole of my foot has become worn through, in holes: see naqiba ]: said to the complainer to him who is in a worse condition than he. (AHei, TA.)

definition: (T, S, M, Msb, K) and maZal~apN , (T, M, Msb, K,) the former with kesr to the m as an instrumental noun, (Msb,) [and the latter with fet-h as a noun of place,] A large tent of [ goats' ] hair;
sourceDefinition: (T, S, M, Msb, K) and maZal~apN , (T, M, Msb, K,) the former with kesr to the m as an instrumental noun, (Msb,) [and the latter with fet-h as a noun of place,] A large tent of [ goats' ] hair; (S, O, Msb;) more ample than the xibaA=' ; so says El-Fárábee: (Msb:) one of the kinds of tents of the Arabs of the desert, the largest of the tents of [ goats' ] hair; next after which is the wasuwT ; and then, the xibaA=' , which is the smallest of the tents of [goats'] hair; so says AZ: but Aboo-Málik says that the mZl~p and the xbA=' are small and large: IAar says that the xayomap is of poles roofed with [the panic grass called] vamaAm , and is not of cloths; but the mZl~p is of cloths: (T:) or it is of the tents called A^axobiyap ; (M;) such as is large, of the A^axobiyap ; (K;) and it is said to be only of cloths; and it is large, having a riwaAq [q. v.]; but sometimes it is of one oblong piece of cloth ( $uq~ap ), and of two such pieces, and of three; and sometimes it has a kifaA=' , which is its hinder part: or, accord. to Th, it is peculiarly of [ goats' ] hair: (M:) see also Zul~apN , and ZuloZulN : the pl. is maZaAl~u ; (M, Msb;) and maZaAli or maZaAliY occurs at the end of a verse of Umeiyeh Ibn-Abee-'Áïdh El-Hudhalee, for maZaAl~i ; the [latter] l being either elided, or changed into Y . (M.) Eil~apN maA Eil~apu A^awotaAdK waA^axil~apK waEamadi AlmiZal~api AuboruzuwA liSihorikumo ↓ Zul~apN [ A pretext: what is the pretext of tentpegs, and of pins for fastening together the edges of the pieces of the tent-cloth, and of the poles of the large tent? go ye forth: he who has married among you has a tent for shade from the sun: ] is a prov., and was said by a girl who had been married to a man, and whose family delayed to conduct her to her husband, urging in excuse that they had not the apparatus of the tent: she said this to urge them, and to put a stop to their excuse: (Meyd, TA: *) and the prov. is applied in attributing untruth to pretexts. (Meyd.) ― -b2- Hence, as being likened thereto, (assumed tropical:) A booth, or shed, made of palm-sticks, and covered with [ the panic grass called ] vumaAm . (Msb.) ― -b3- And The thing [i. e. umbrella ] by means of which kings are shaded on the occasion of their riding; called in Pers. Jator . (TA.)

(Az.)

definition: Small long hairs under the part beneath the lower jaw of the camel: (S, K:) [pl.
sourceDefinition: Small long hairs under the part beneath the lower jaw of the camel: (S, K:) [pl. EavaAniynu :] one says baEiyrN *uw EavaAniyna [ a camel having such small long hairs ], like as they said, for the maforiq of the head, mafaAriqu . (S.) And The beard: or the portion thereof that extends beyond the two sides of the cheeks: or the portion that grows upon the chin and beneath it, downwards: or length of the beard: (K:) or the portion of the beard that depends form the chin: (Ham p. 820:) and Euvonuwnu All~iHoyapi signifies the extremity of the beard. (TA.) And Certain small hairs at the part in which the he-goat is slaughtered. (TA.) And The raEovap [or wattle ] of the cock. (S and K in art. rEv , q. v.) ― -b2- Also The first of wind and of rain; (S, K;) so says [the Imám] Aboo- Haneefeh: (TA:) or rain generally: or rain while it is between the heaven and the earth: pl.
