EuvonuwnN : (S, TA:) and Euvonuwnu Als~aHaAbi signifies the clouds that have fallen upon the earth: and EavaAniynu Als~aHaAbi the pendent skirts of the clouds: and Euvonuwnu Alr~iyHi the trail of the wind when it comes drawing along the dust: pl. as above. (TA.) And The first of anything. (Ham p. 820.)

sourceDefinition: (S, K, &c.) and ↓ EajaAwapN and ↓ EajaAyapN , or ↓ EujaAwapN and ↓ EujaAyapN , (accord. to different copies of the K, [but in the TA these two words are expl. only as in another paragraph which will be found below,]) A sort of dates in El-Medeeneh, (S, K,) of the best kind, the palm-tree of which is called liynapN ; (S; [or, accord. to Fr and Akh, cited in the TA in art. lwn , the term liynapN is applied to a palm-tree but not to that of the Eajowap ;]) said to be from what was planted by the hand of the Prophet; accord. to IAth, they are larger than the SayoHaAniY~ [q. v.], inclining to blackness; but accord. to Az, the Eajowap in El-Medeeneh are the SayoHaAniy~ap , and there are sorts of the Ejwp there that have not the sweetness nor the odour nor the fulness of the SyHAny~p : (TA:) or the best of dates: (Mgh:) and, in El-Hijáz, the dates that are stuffed ( maHo$iY~ ) [or pressed into a compact mass, while moist, in the receptacle of palm-leaves or skin, as are the dates called Eajowap in the present day]; (K, TA;) they are termed A^um~u Alt~amori [lit. the mother of dates, app. because many persons keep a stock thereof], to which recourse is had, like the [ dates called ] $ihoriyz in El-Basrah. (TA.)

definition: and ↓ AlEujaAwapu are two dial.
sourceDefinition: and ↓ AlEujaAwapu are two dial. vars., each signifying A piece of the size of a gobbet of flesh, conjoined with a sinew ( EaSabap ) which descends from the knee of the camel to the foot: (As, S, TA:) or the EujaAyataAni are two sinews ( EaSabataAni ) in the interior of the fore legs of the horse, in the lower parts of which are things resembling nails ( A^aZofaAr ), called Als~aEodaAnaAt : and EujaAyapN is a term applied to all sinews ( EaSab ) that conjoin with the solid hoof: (S, TA:) or it signifies certain sinews ( EaSab ) in which are set ossicles resembling the gems that are set in signet-rings, at the pastern of the horse, or similar beast; (K, TA;) when one is hungry, he bruises them between two stones, and eats them; and ↓ EujaAwapN is a dial. var. thereof: (TA:) or any sinew ( EaSabap ) in a fore leg ( yad ) or in a hind leg ( rijol ): or a sinew ( EaSabap ) in the interior of the shank ( waZiyf ) of the horse and of the bull: (K, TA:) or, in a horse, the sinew ( Eaqabap ) extending lengthwise from the shank and ending at each of the pasterns; and in it is what is termed AlxTm [a mistranscription, correctly AlHaTam , which means a certain disease in the leg]: and in a she-camel, a sinew ( Eaqabap ) in the interior of her fore leg: and also in a horse, a piece of flesh like a small gobbet: accord. to IAth, AlEujaAyaAtu signifies the sinews ( A^aEoSaAb ) of the legs of camels and of horses: (TA:) pl. EujFY (S, K) and EujiY~N and EajaAyaA (K) and EujaAyaA and EujaAyaAtN . (TA.) -A2- See also the first paragraph.

definition: Punishment, castigation, or chastisement, [or] such as serves to give warning to others than the sufferer, or to restrain the offender from repeating the offence;
sourceDefinition: Punishment, castigation, or chastisement, [or] such as serves to give warning to others than the sufferer, or to restrain the offender from repeating the offence; syn. EuquwbapN , (S, O,) or nakaAlN : (K, and Ksh and Bd in ii. 6:) so termed from Ea*aba “ he prevented ” &c.; because it prevents the person punished from returning to the like of his offence, and prevents others from doing the like of that which he has done: (MF, TA:) [it generally signifies any corporal punishment: ] and, by an extension of the original signification, any [ infliction of ] pain that disgraces, or puts to shame: (Ksh and Bd ubi suprà:) originally, beating: afterwards used to signify any painful punishment: [ torture; or torment: ] and metaphorically applied to (tropical:) an affair, or event, that is difficult, distressing, afflicting, or troublesome; whence the saying, Als~afaru qiToEapN mina AlEa*aAbi [ Travel is a portion of that which is difficult, &c.; or of torment ]: (Msb:) in the Kur xxiii. 78, it means hunger, or famine: (Zj, O, TA:) the pl. is A^aEo*ibapN : (Zj, K, TA:) the author of the K says in art. nhr [voce nahaArN ] that it has no pl.: [and it seems to be doubted whether it have a pl. because it is properly an inf. n. though its verb in the unaugmented form is not used:] but MF observes that if it be a name for that whereby one is prevented [from repeating an offence], as hunger, or famine, agreeably with what Zj says, there is no reason why it should not have this pl. (TA.)

definition: and ↓ Ea*uwbN , applied to a horse or the like, &c.
sourceDefinition: and ↓ Ea*uwbN , applied to a horse or the like, &c., (S, O,) Such as is standing still, or stopping from fatigue, ( qaAy^imN , S,) that will not eat nor drink: (S, O:) or abstaining, or that abstains, from eating, by reason of intense thirst; (K, TA;) applied to a man, and an ass, and a horse: but Az says that the assertion respecting these two epithets that they signify [a horse, &c.] that neither eats nor drinks is more correct than the assertion respecting ↓ Ea*uwbN that it signifies [one] that abstains from eating by reason of his thirst: also, that EaA*ibN signifies any animal, but generally a horse and a camel, that will not eat anything: accord. to Th, this and ↓ Ea*uwbN signify a horse or the like standing still, or stopping from fatigue, ( qaAy^imN ,) that raises his head, and will not eat nor drink; and the former, that passes a night without eating anything: (TA:) the pl. of EaA*ibN is Eu*uwbN , like as sujuwdN is a pl. of saAjidN : and the pl. of ↓ Ea*uwbN is Eu*ubN , and, accord. to A 'Obeyd, Eu*uwbN [like as hujuwdN is pl. of hajuwdN ]: Az says that this is a mistake, for a word of the measure faEuwlN does not form a pl. of the measure fuEuwlN ; but [SM says] this is an extr. instance; and he who preserves an authority in his mind is an evidence against him who does not. (TA.) One says, ↓ baAta Ea*uwbFA , meaning He passed the night without eating or drinking anything; because abstaining therefrom. (O.) ― -b2- EaA*ibN signifies also [ Unsheltered; ] having no covering between him and the sky; (O, K;) and so ↓ Ea*uwbN . (K, TA.) El-Jaadee says, describing a wild bull ( vawor waHo$iY~ [a species of bovine antelope]) that had passed the night alone, tasting nothing, lils~amaA='i kaA^an~ahu ↓ fabaAta Ea*uwbFA suhayolN A_i*aA maA A^aforadatohu AlkawaAkibu [ And he passed the night exposed without shelter to the sky, as though he were Canopus when the other stars have left him solitary ]. (TA.)

definition: A callousness in the hind leg of a horse or similar beast, above the pastern, in the hinder part thereof;
sourceDefinition: A callousness in the hind leg of a horse or similar beast, above the pastern, in the hinder part thereof; and it is what is called $uqaAq [q. v.]: and, as ISk says, purulent pustules ( qaroH ) that arise in the neck of a camel, in consequence of which he scratches, or scrapes, himself, and sometimes he lies down against the stem of a tree and scratches, or scrapes, himself therewith; and its cure, he says, is the burning of fat upon him. (S:) and an eruption like pustules, or purulent pustules, in the necks of young weaned camels, in consequence of which they scratch, or scrape, themselves: (IB, TA:) or, as also ↓ EuronapN and ↓ EiraAnN , a certain disease in the hinder part of the hind leg of a horse or similar beast, (K, TA,) like an abrasion in the skin, (TA,) causing the hair to fall off: or a cracking, or chapping, (K, TA,) incident to horse, (TA,) in their fore legs and their hind legs: or a callousness that arises in the pastern of a horse (K, TA) or similar beast, and in the place of its fetlock, in the hinder part, and a $uqaAq [q. v.] that betides it from the kicking against a mountain or stone. (TA.) -A2- Also The foul smell, or foulness [of the hands] with the smell, of flesh-meat and its grease; syn. gamarN : (K:) so in the saying, A^ajidu raAy^iHapa Earani yadayoka [ I perceive the odour of the foulness of thy hands with the smell of flesh-meat and its grease ]: (IAar, TA:) or EaranN signifies the odour of flesh-meat that has Earom [i. e. grease, or gravy ]: and also i. q. Earom [ itself, q. v.]. (TA.) And The odour of cooked flesh-meat; (Kr, K;) as also ↓ EironN . (K.) And A mark, or relic, [or soil, ] of broth upon the hand of the cater. (El-Hejeree, TA.) And Cooked flesh-meat: (IAar, K:) or, as some say, flesh, or flesh-meat, in an absolute sense. (TA.) ― -b2- And Smoke. (K.) -A3- Also A species of tree, with which one tans. (K.) Dioscorides asserts the Ern to be A plant having leaves resembling those of the small lentil, except that they are longer than they, and having a stem about a span tall, and a red flower, and a small root; growing in neglected, or uncultivated, places: a poultice of its leaves with olive-oil is sudorific; its bruised leaves applied as a poultice act as a discutient to wounds and inflamed pustules; and taken in a beverage. or sirup, they cure the dribbling of the urine. (Avicenna, i. e. Ibn-Seenà book ii. p. 235.)

definition: One who prostrates, or throws down, his antagonists much, or often;
sourceDefinition: One who prostrates, or throws down, his antagonists much, or often; with whom one cannot cope: (S, K, TA: [in the CK, AlSariyEu is erroneously put for AlS~ir~iyEu :]) accord. to IB, as signifying Sir~iyEN , it is used in commendation: Fr says that when a man is one who prostrates, or throws down, his antagonists much, or often, abominable, wicked, or crafty, [ with whom one cannot cope, ] it is said that he is EironapN laA yuTaAqu . (TA.) ― -b2- Also A man coarse, rough, or rude, and niggardly. (TA.) ― -b3- And One who serves houses, or tents. (TA.) -A2- Also The roots of the Earanotun , (AA, S, TA, in the K, erroneously, of the Eironiyn , TA,) which is a plant used for tanning. (S in art. Ertn .) ― -b2- And The wood of the Zimax , (S, K,) a species of tree, (S, TA,) having the form of the dulob [or plane-tree ], (TA,) with which skins for water or milk are tanned, (S, K,) and from which is cut the wood of the beaters and washers and whiteners of clothes, which is buried: accord. to ISk, [but the same is also said of the Earotun ,] it is a species of tree resembling the Eawosaj [or box-thorn ], except that it is bigger than it, full and luxuriant in the branch, and not having tall stems: (TA:) or it is called ↓ EironN , [which is a coll. gen. n.,] and EironapN is the n. un. (AA, T in art. Zmx .) And [it is also expl. as signifying] The piece of wood of the beaters and washers and whiteners of clothes upon which the beating is performed with that which is called the miyjanap . (IKh, TA.)

definition: The first part or portion of anything.
sourceDefinition: The first part or portion of anything. (S, Msb, K.) ― -b2- And hence, (Msb,) [particularly,] the first [or upper ] part [i. e. the bridge ] of the nose, beneath the place where the eyebrows come together; the place of what is termed Al$~amamu : (S, Msb, TA:) or the head of the nose: (TA:) or the hard part of the bone of the nose: (K:) or it signifies, (K,) or is sometimes applied to, (Msb,) the nose, (Msb, K,) altogether: (K:) pl. EaraAniynu . (TA.) One says, humo $um~u AlEaraAniyni [ They are high in respect of the noses, or of the bridges thereof; often meaning (assumed tropical:) they are haughty, or disdainful ]. (S, Msb.) Hence also, EaraAniynu Als~aHaAbi The first of the rains of the clouds. EurunN . (TA.)

definition: The nest of a bird, formed of what it collects together, (S, A, Mgh, O, Msb, K,) of slender pieces of sticks, (S, A, O, K,) &c.
sourceDefinition: The nest of a bird, formed of what it collects together, (S, A, Mgh, O, Msb, K,) of slender pieces of sticks, (S, A, O, K,) &c., (S, O,) or of fragments of sticks, (Mgh, Msb,) in which it lays its eggs, (Mgh,) in a tree, (S, A, Mgh, O, Msb, K,) in the branches thereof; (S, A, O, K;) as also ↓ Ea$~N : (A, K:) but if in a mountain, (S, O, Msb,) or a building, (Msb,) or a wall or the like, (S, O,) it is called wakorN , and wakonN ; and if in the ground, A^ufoHuwSN , (S, O, Msb,) and A^udoHiY~N : (S, O:) or the nest of a raven or other bird, upon a tree, when it is dense, or compact, and large: (Lth, T:) pl. [of pauc.] A^aEo$aA$N (S, Msb) and [of mult.] Ei$aA$N and Ei$a$apN (S, Mgh, Msb) and Eu$uw$N . (TA.) [See also Eu$oEu$N .] It is said in a prov., quoted in a xuTobap of El-Hajjáj, (O, TA,) layosa h`*aA biEu$~iki faA@dorujiY [(assumed tropical:) This is not thy nest, or] thou hast no right in this; therefore go thy way: (A, O, K: *) addressed to him who alights in a place of abode not befitting him: (A, TA:) or to him who raises himself above his rank: and to him who applies himself to a thing not of his business to do: and to him who is at case in an improper time; wherefore he is thus ordered to be diligent and in motion. (TA.) And in another prov., (TA,) talam~aso A^aEo$aA$aka (assumed tropical:) Seek thou, or seek thou repeatedly, after pretexts, and [ causes for ] false accusation, in thy family (O, L, K, TA) and those belonging to thee: (TA:) [not in others: (see Freytag's Arab. Prov., i. 235:)] nearly like the former proverb. (TA.) [In the CK, talam~asa is erroneously put for talam~aso .]

sourceDefinition: , and EaDiDotu Ealayohi , (S, O, Msb, K,) and bihi (S, O, Msb,) third pers. EaD~a , (S,) aor. , (S, Msb, K,) i. e. yaEaD~u , (ISk, S, O,) imp. EaD~ [i. e. EaD~a and EaD~i ] and AiEoDaDN , (TA,) inf. n. EaD~N (Mgh, O, Msb, K) and EaDiyDN (O, K) and EuDaADN , (TA, [see also EiDaADN , below,]) [ I bit it; or] I seized it, or took hold of it, with my teeth, (A, Mgh, Msb, K,) and pressed it therewith; (TA;) namely, a thing, (A,) or a morsel of food: (S, Msb:) or with my tongue; (A, K;) as, for instance, a serpent does; but not a scorpion; for this latter stings: (TA:) accord. to the Book of Verbs by IKtt, one also says EaDaDotu , aor. : (Msb:) and [it has been asserted that] one says, (Msb, K,) though rarely, (Msb,) EaDaDotu , aor. : (Msb, K:) it is said in the S [and O] that ISk cites AO as asserting that EaDaDotu , with fet-h [to the first D ] is a dial. var. [which obtained] among [the tribes of] Er-Ribáb: but, IB says, this is a mistranscription; for what ISk says, in the book entitled “ ElIsláh, ” is, gaSiSotu biAll~uqomapi faA^anaA A^agaS~u bihaA gaSaSFA qaAla A^abuw Eubayodapa wagaSaSotu lugapN fiY Alr~ibaAbi , with [the pointed g and] the unpointed S : to which [says SM] I add, that thus it is found in the handwriting of Aboo-Zekereeyà and of Ibn-El-Jawáleekee, in the “ Isláh ” of ISk, and they expressly assert that what is in the S is a mistranscription. (TA.) ― -b2- EaD~a Alfarasu EalaY lijaAmihi [ The horse champed his bit ]. (Msb.) ― -b3- It is said in the Kur [iii. 115], waA_i*aA xalawoA EaD~awA Ealayokumu AlA^anaAmila mina AlgayoZi (assumed tropical:) [ And when they are alone, they bite the ends of the fingers by reason of wrath, or rage, against you ]: meaning that, by reason of the vehemence of their hatred of the believers, they eat [or rather bite] their hands in wrath, or rage. (O, TA.) You say also, EaD~a EalaY yadihi gayoZFA (tropical:) [ He bit his hand in wrath, or rage ], when a man is inordinate in his enmity. (TA.) In like manner, it is said in the Kur [xxv. 29], wayawoma yaEaD~u AlZ~aAlimu EalaY yadayohi (tropical:) [ And the day when the wrong-doer shall bite his hands ]; meaning, in repentance and regret. (O, TA.) And it is said in a prov., EaD~a EalaY $ibodiEihi , i. e. lisaAnihi (assumed tropical:) [ He bit his tongue ]: applied to the clement, or forbearing. (O, TA.) One says also, EaD~a biAloxamosi , meaning He bit the fingers. (Ham p. 790.) ― -b4- EaD~a fiY AlEilomi binaAji*ihi (tropical:) He confirmed his knowledge; made it sound. (Mgh.) ― -b5- Mohammad said, Ealayokumo bisun~atiY wasun~api AlxulafaA='i Alr~a$idiyna mino baEodiY EaD~uwA EalayohaA biAln~awaAji*i , meaning (assumed tropical:) [ Keep ye to my course of conduct, and the course of conduct of the orthodox Khaleefehs after me: ] cleave ye, or hold ye fast, thereto. (Mgh, * Msb.) And you say, of a man, EaD~a biSaAHibihi , (S, O, K,) aor. , (S,) inf. n. EaDiyDN (S, O, K) and EaD~N , (TA,) (assumed tropical:) He kept, or clave, to his companion; (S, O, K;) he stuck to him: (TA:) and EaD~ahu has the same, which is said to be the primary, signification; (TA;) or this signifies he seized him with his teeth, because the doing so is a means of cleaving. (IAth, TA.) You say also EDDt bimaAliY , [so in the TA, without any vowel-signs to the verb,] inf. n. EuDuwDapN and EaDaADapN , [to agree with which, the pret. by rule should be EaDuDotu ,] (assumed tropical:) I clave, or held fast, to my property. (TA.) And EaD~a fulaAnN biAl$~ar~i (tropical:) Such a one kept, or clave, to evil, or mischief, and did not leave it. (A, TA.) ― -b6- EaD~ahu , (Aboo-'Is-hák, TA in art. hmz ,) or EaD~ahu bilisaAnihi , (A, TA, *) inf. n. EaD~N , (TA,) (tropical:) He defamed him; spoke evil of him; or backbit him. (Aboo-Is-hák, ubi suprà; A, TA.) ― -b7- EaD~a Alv~iqaAfu biA^anaAbiybi Alr~umoHi , and EaD~a EalayohaA , inf. n. EaD~N , (tropical:) The straighteninginstrument held fast to [or pinched ] the internodal portions of the spear. (TA.) ― -b8- EaD~ahu Alqatabu , inf. n. EaD~N , (tropical:) [ The camel's saddle hurt him ] as though it bit him. (IB.) ― -b9- EaD~ahumu Als~ilaAHu (tropical:) [ The weapon, or weapons, wounded them ]. (O, TA.) ― -b10- EaD~ahu AlA^amoru (tropical:) The thing, or affair, was, or became, severe, or distressing, or afflictive, to him. (A, TA.) And you say also, EaD~atohu AlHarobu (A, O) and EaD~ato bihi (tropical:) War, or the war, was, or became, severe to him. (Ham p. 628. See an ex. voce raHiymN .) EaD~u Alz~amaAni and AlHarobi signify (tropical:) The severity, or rigour, of time, or fortune, and of war: or in these two cases, the former word is with Z : (K:) or, accord. to IKtt and others, EaD~ and EaZ~ are two dial. vars. (TA.) And EaD~a , aor. , inf. n. EaDiyDN , signifies also (assumed tropical:) He, or it, was, or became, strong, or hard; syn. Ai$otad~a and Saluba : (IKtt, TA:) app. said of a man: (TA:) [or, thus used, it has a more comprehensive meaning; for] it is said in the S that EaDiDota , addressed to a man, signifies (tropical:) thou becamest, or hast become, such as is termed EiD~N [q. v.]; and the like is said in the A; and Sgh adds [in the O] that its inf. n. is EaDaADapN . (TA.) ― -b11- EaD~atohu AlA^asofaAru (tropical:) Travels rendered him experienced, or expert. (A, TA.) And one says, EaD~atohu AlA^amuwru biA^aDoraAsihaA waA^akalatohu Hat~aY Ear~afatohu (assumed tropical:) [ The management of affairs rendered him experienced so that they taught him ]. (A in art. jrs .)

definition: , inf. n. taEoDiyDN , [ He bit him, or it, much, or frequently, ] a word of the dial. of Temeem. (TA.) You say, fulaAnN yuEaD~iDu $afatayohi Such a one bites ( yaEaD~u ) his lips much, or often, by...
sourceDefinition: , inf. n. taEoDiyDN , [ He bit him, or it, much, or frequently, ] a word of the dial. of Temeem. (TA.) You say, fulaAnN yuEaD~iDu $afatayohi Such a one bites ( yaEaD~u ) his lips much, or often, by reason of anger. (S.) And, of an ass, EaD~aDatohu AlHumuru The asses bit him much, (O, K,) and lacerated him with their teeth. (O.) ― -b2- [And hence,] ED~D He jested with his girl, or young woman. (IAar, O, K.) -A2- Also ED~D , (inf. n. as above, IAar,) (assumed tropical:) He drew water from a well such as is termed EaDuwDN . (IAar, O, K.) -A3- And He fed his camels with [ the provender termed ] EuD~ . (IAar, O, K.)

definition: I made him to bite the thing;
sourceDefinition: I made him to bite the thing; or to seize it, or take hold of it, with his teeth. (S, * O, K.) ― -b2- It is said in a trad., mano taEaz~aY biEazaA='i AljaAhiliy~api faA^aEiD~uwhu bihani A^abiyhi walaA takonuwA (S, * Mgh, Msb, K) i. e. Whoso asserteth his relationship [ of son ] in the manner of the people of the Time of Ignorance, meaning by saying, in crying out for aid or succour, yaA lafulaAnK , (Mgh and Msb in art. Ezw ,) and exclaiming, A^anaA fulaAnu bonu fulaAnK , (Msb,) say ye to him AiEoDaDo biA^ayori A^abiyka , (Mgh, O, L, Msb,) or AEDD A^ayora A^abiyka , (K,) [ Bite thou the Ayr of thy father, ] and use not a metonymical term for it, by saying hn for Ayr . (Mgh, O, L, K.) ― -b3- A^aEoDaDotuhu sayofiY (tropical:) [ I made my sword to wound him; ] I smote him with my sword. (S, O, K.) And A^aEaD~a Als~ayofa bisaAqi AlbaEiyri (tropical:) [ He made the sword to wound the thigh, or shank, of the camel ]. (A, TA.) And A^aEaD~a AlmaHaAjima qafaAhu (Lh, A, O *) (tropical:) He made the cupping-instruments to cleave to the back of his neck. (Lh.) -A2- A^aEaD~ati Albiy^oru (assumed tropical:) The well became such as is termed EaDuwDN . (S, O, K.) -A3- A^aEaD~uwA Their camels ate [ the provender called ] EuD~ : (S, O, K:) and their camels pastured upon [ the trees called ] EiD~ , (S, O,) or EaDaAD . (L.) ― -b2- And AED~t AlA^aroDu The land abounded with EiD~ , (S, O,) or EuD~ , (K,) or both. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: [is of the measure fiEolN , in the sense of the measure faAEilN in some cases, and in the sense of the measure mafoEuwlN in other cases; but appears to have only tropical significations]. ― -b2- (tropical:) A lock that will scarcely open; or that is not near to opening; expl. by laA yakaAdu yanofatiHu : (S, A, O, K:) or that will not open. (TA.) ― -b3- (tropical:) One who keeps close to his property: (TA:) a man who improves his means of subsistence and his property, attends closely to it, and manages it well: (L:) or a manager of property: (K:) or EiD~u maAlK signifies one who manages property well: (A:) or who manages property rigorously. (S, O.) ― -b4- (tropical:) Niggardly, tenacious, or avaricious: (K, TA:) for a man's keeping close to his property generally courses him to fall into niggardliness: or such a person is likened to a lock that will not open. Haz~N . (K accord. to the TA.) laA taEolubo Suwrataka i. e. Make not thou a mark upon thy Swrp [here meaning face, as in some other instances,] occurs in a trad., as said to a man upon whose nose was seen a mark [of dust, or an impression,] made by pressing hard upon it in prostration. (O, TA.) -A2- Ealaba Als~ayofa , aor. (S, O, K) and , (K,) inf. n. (TA.) ― -b2- [And Euliba seems to signify sometimes It was tied with, or by, a sinew, or tendon: see a usage of its part. n. voce matonN .] -A3- Ealiba , [aor. ,] (TA,) inf. n. (TA.) -A5- And Ealiba , aor. , inf. n. EalabN ; and Ealaba , aor. , inf. n. EalobN ; It was, or became, hard, or firm; (O, K;) and hard, tough, or coarse: (K:) each, said of flesh, or flesh-meat, and of a plant, has the former meaning: (O:) or the latter verb, said of flesh, or flesh-meat, has that meaning; and the former verb, said of a plant, has the latter meaning: (S:) or the former verb, said of flesh, or flesh-meat, means it was, or became, hard, or firm, and thick, or coarse; and the latter verb also, it was, or became, thick, or coarse, and hard, not soft, or tender. (Suh, TA.) And Ealibato yaduhu His hand was, or became, thick, coarse, or rough. (TA.) [See also 10.] ― -b2- And Ealiba , aor. , inf. n. EalabN ; and Ealaba , aor. ; and ↓ AstElb ; said of flesh-meat, It became altered in odour [ for the worse ], after having been hard, or firm. (K.)

definition: A milking-vessel of skin, (S, O, TA,) or of wood, like a large qadaH [or bowl ]: (TA:) or a large qadaH of camel's skin, or of wood, into which one milks: (K:) or a bowl into which the she-camel is...
sourceDefinition: A milking-vessel of skin, (S, O, TA,) or of wood, like a large qadaH [or bowl ]: (TA:) or a large qadaH of camel's skin, or of wood, into which one milks: (K:) or a bowl into which the she-camel is milked: or a qadaH of wood, or of skin and wood: or a vessel of skin, in the form of a bowl, with a wooden hoop: Az says, it is a piece of skin taken from the side of a camel's hide while it is fresh; it is made round, and filled with soft sand; then its edges are drawn together, and perforated with a wooden skewer, and it is bound so as to be closed, [ thus ] contracted, by a cord [ passed through the holes made with the skewer ], and left until it becomes dry and tough; then its upper part is cut off, and it stands by reason of its dryness, resembling a round bowl, as though it were carved out, or fashioned by the turner; the pastor and the rider suspend it, and milk into it, and drink out of it; and it is convenient to the man of the desert by its lightness, and its not breaking when the camel shakes it about or when it falls to the ground: (TA:) IAar says that this word and janobapN and dasomaA='u and samoraA='u all signify the same: (O:) the pl. is EulabN (S, O, Msb, K) and EilaAbN . (S, Msb, K.) -A2- Also A tall palm-tree: (O, K:) [see ↓ EulobN (voce saAjidN ), a coll. gen. n. used as a pl.; or a pl., and, if so, app. a contraction of EulabN , by poetic license: Sgh, however, adds,] but some say that it is ↓ EalabapN [i. e.] biAlt~aHoriyk . (O.)

definition: [perfectly decl.
sourceDefinition: [perfectly decl., because the ' is a letter of quasi-coordination, i. e., added to render the word quasi-coordinate to the class of qiroTaAsN and the like,] The EaSab of the neck; [app. meaning the upper, cervical, tendinous portion of the trapezius muscle; ] (S, O, K; [in all of which, mention is made of the ElbA=' of the camel, to which it seems to be most commonly applied, and also to that of a man;]) it is one of a pair, and between one ElbA=' and the other is the place of growth of the mane; (S, O;) Az explains it as specially applied to the thick EaSab ; and IAth, as the EaSab in the neck, extending to the kaAhil [or part between the two shoulder-blades ]: ISd says that it is syn. with EaqabN [q. v.]: (TA:) [it is also said that] it signifies the EaSabap [i. e. tendon, or sinew, ] that extends in the neck: (Msb:) or the yellow EaSabap in the side ( SafoHap ) of the neck; one of a pair: (A:) and the EilobaAwaAni in a man are [said to be] the two yellow tendons or sinews ( AlEaSabataAni AlS~aforaAwaAni ) in the maton [or part next the spine, on either side, ] of the neck: (Zj in his “ Khalk el-Insán: ”) [but of all the meanings thus assigned to it, the first seems to be the most proper, or at least the most usual: see Q. Q. 1:] the Arabs used to bind therewith, in the fresh, or moist, state, the A^ajofaAn [or sheaths] of their swords, and also their spears when cracked, and it dried upon them, and became strong: (IAth, TA:) the word is masc., (Lh, TA,) or [it is masc. and fem., but] the making it fem. is preferred [though this is contr. to analogy]: (Msb:) the dual is EilobaAwaAni (S, A, O, Msb) and EilobaA A=ni ; (S, O, Msb, K;) [the former app. the more common, but the latter the more proper;] for the ' [in the sing.] is a letter of quasi-coordination [and therefore properly with tenween]; but if you will, you may liken it to the fem. ' that is in HamoraA='u [of which the dual is more properly HamoraAwaAni ], or to the radical ' [or rather the ' that is substituted for the last radical letter] in kisaA='N [of which the dual is more pro- perly kisaA A=ni ]: (S, O:) and the pl. is EalaAbiY~u . (S, O, K.) You say of a man when he has become advanced in age, ta$an~aja EilobaA='u Alr~ajuli [ The ElbA=' of the man has become contracted ]. (S, O.) ― -b2- The pl. EalaAbiY~u is expl. in the K as signifying also Lead: and in the S as signifying lead, or a kind thereof: (TA:) El-Kutabee says, “ I have been told that AlEalaAbiY~u signifies lead; but I am not sure of it: ” and Az says, “ I know not any one who has said it, and it is not true; ” (O, TA;) and this is the case: (O:) MF observes that its explanation as signifying lead requires it to be a sing. of a pl. form, or a pl. that has no sing., like A^abaAbiylu and EabaAdiydu : (TA:) in a trad., mention is made of swords of which the ornaments were AlElAbY~ and AlA=nuk ; (O, TA;) and the coupling of these two words together has led to the supposition that the former means lead; but there is no evading the fact that it is the pl. of ElbaA=' meaning the EaSab of the camel. (TA.)

definition: [ Ambergris; ] a certain odoriferous substance, (S, O, Msb, K,) well known; (O, Msb;) an excrement found in the belly of a certain great fish, [ the spermaceti-whale, ] which is called by the same...
sourceDefinition: [ Ambergris; ] a certain odoriferous substance, (S, O, Msb, K,) well known; (O, Msb;) an excrement found in the belly of a certain great fish, [ the spermaceti-whale, ] which is called by the same name; (Towsheeh, TA;) or an excrement of a certain marine beast; (K;) or, accord. to Ks, a vegetable [ substance found ] in the bottom of the sea and driven by the waves to the shores thereof, whence it is taken; (O;) or, (O, K,) as the physicians say, (O,) it issues from a source in the sea; (O, * K;) [and there are other opinions respecting its origin, mentioned in the TA; but these I do not add, as it is well known to be an excrement of the spermaceti-whale;] the best kind is the white, and the whitish; next, the blue [or gray ]; and the worst, the black: (TA:) the word is masc. and fem., (AA, IAmb, O, Msb,) like misokN : (IAmb, TA voce *akiY~N :) MF says that most hold the n to be augmentative, the measure being fanoEalN , as it is said to be in the Msb. (TA.) ― -b2- [As mentioned above, it signifies also The spermaceti-whale; ] a certain great fish; (Msb in art. Ebr ;) a certain marine fish, (Az, O, K,) the length of which reaches to fifty cubits, called in Pers. PAlh [app. a mistranscription for waAlo : see baAlN ]: (Az, TA:) shields are made of its skin; (Mgh, O, TA;) and the people of Juddeh have sandals, or shoes, made thereof. (O, TA.) ― -b3- And hence, (O,) A shield (S, O, K) made of the skin of the fish above-mentioned: (O, K:) and some say, coats of defence ( duruwE ). (O.) -A2- Also Saffron. (K.) ― -b2- And (as some say, TA) [The plant called ] waros . (K.) ― -b3- [Accord. to Forskål (Flora Aegypt. Arab. p. lxiv.) now applied to Gomphrena globosa. ] -A3- See also the next paragraph, in two places.

sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. EanojN , He drew, or pulled, anything; drew it, or pulled it, to him, or towards him. (L.) ― -b2- Eanaja raA^osa AlbaEiyri , aor. and , inf. n. as above, He (the rider) pulled up, or drew up, the camel's head by means of the [ halter, or cord, called ] xiTaAm . (TA.) And Eanaja AlbaEiyra , aor. , (S, O,) inf. n. EanojN as above; (S, O, K;) and ↓ AEnjhu , (O,) inf. n. A_iEonaAjN ; (K;) He trained, or broke, the camel in a certain manner; (S, O;) i. e. he (the rider) pulled, or drew, the camel's xiTaAm (S, O, K, TA) towards his head, (TA,) and forced him back upon his hind legs, (S, O, K, TA,) so that, sometimes, the prominent part behind his ears clave to the upright piece of wood that rises from the fore part of the saddle: (TA:) and Eanaja Aljamala He pulled the nose-rein of the camel to make him stop: and Eanaja Aln~aAqapa He reined up the she-camel on an occasion of her stumbling. (TA, from trads.) ― -b3- Eanaja Ald~alowa , (IAar, S, O, L,) aor. , (L,) inf. n. as above; (S, O;) and ↓ AEnjhA ; (IAar, O;) He put, or attached, to the leathern bucket, an appertenance called EinaAj [q. v.]. (IAar, S, O, L.) ― -b4- And hence, Eanajotu Albakora , aor. , inf. n. as above, I tied the young camel's [ halter, or cord, called ] xiTaAm to his arm, and made it short: thus one does to a young camel only when he is trained, or broken. (TA.) ― -b5- Eanajahu also signifies, He bent it, or inclined it; and occurs in this sense in a trad. of 'Alee, in which the pronoun relates to a sail. (TA.) definition: A rope, or cord, (S, A, O, K,) or girth, (S, O,) or strap, (TA,) that is tied to the lower part of the large [ leathern bucket called ] dalow , (S, O, K,) or that is put beneath the dlw , (A,) and...
sourceDefinition: A rope, or cord, (S, A, O, K,) or girth, (S, O,) or strap, (TA,) that is tied to the lower part of the large [ leathern bucket called ] dalow , (S, O, K,) or that is put beneath the dlw , (A,) and then tied to the cross-pieces of wood ( AlEaraAqiY ), (S, A, O, K,) or to the loops, (TA,) so that it serves as an aid to the cross-pieces of wood and to the [ thongs called ] wa*am [ which bind those cross-pieces to the loops of the bucket ]; for when these [ thongs ] break, it holds fast the dlw : (S, O:) and when the dlw is light, (S, O, K,) it is a string, (S, O,) or a light string, (K,) that is tied from one of the loops to one of the cross-pieces of wood ( AlErAqY ): (S, O, K:) or, as some say, a loop in the lower part of the bucket, inside it, which is tied by a cord or the like to the upper part of the [ rope called ] karab [q. v.], so that if the rope [meaning the krb , not the main rope,] break, it keeps the bucket from falling in the well: this is when the bucket is light: pl. [of pauc.] A^aEonijapN and [of mult.] EunujN . (TA.) One says, laA bud~a lild~aA='i mino EilaAjK walild~ilaA='i mino EinaAjK [ It is absolutely necessary for the disease to have medical treatment, and for the buckets to have an EnAj ]. (A, TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] El-Hotei-ah says, (S, O, TA,) praising a people, or party, who concluded a covenant with their neighbour and faithfully kept it, (TA,) qawomN A_i*aA EaqaduwA EaqodFA lijaArihimu $ad~uwA AlEinaAja wa$ad~uwA fawoqahu AlkarabaA (assumed tropical:) [ A people who, when they conclude a covenant with their neighbour, (lit. tie a knot to their neighbour, ) tie the EnAj , and tie above it the krb : i. e. make it doubly sure]. (S, O, TA.) ― -b3- [Hence also,] qawolN laA EinaAja lahu (tropical:) The support, or foundation, of the affair; that upon which the affair rests, or whereby it subsists. (A, O, L, TA. [In the K, waAlA^amoru wamilaAkuhu is erroneously put for wamina AlA^amori milaAkuhu ; as is said in the TA.]) Thus in the saying, laA A^adoriY liA^amorika EinaAjFA (assumed tropical:) [ I know not any foundation to thine affair ]. (O.) And EinaAju AlA^amori A_ilaY A^aYi sufoyaAna , occurring in a trad., means (assumed tropical:) The management of the affair pertained to Aboo-Sufyán; he being to his companions like the EnAj that bears the weight of the bucket. (TA.) ― -b4- EinaAjN signifies also A thing with which one draws, or pulls. (TA.) ― -b5- And The nose-rein ( zimaAm ) of a she-camel; because she is drawn, or pulled, by means of it. (A, TA.) ― -b6- See also 4. ― -b7- Also Pain of the Sulob [meaning back-bone, or loins, ] (O, K) and of the joints. (O.)

definition: He renewed his acquaintance with it, or his knowledge of it;
sourceDefinition: He renewed his acquaintance with it, or his knowledge of it; (S, O, L, Msb, K;) this is the proper signification; (Msb;) as also ↓ AEthdhu ; (O, * L, K;) and ↓ tEAhdhu ; (L, K;) and ↓ EAhdhu , inf. n. muEaAhadapN : (L:) and he sought it, or sought for it or after it, it being absent from him; syn. tafaq~adahu ; as also ↓ tEAhdhu , and ↓ AEthdh : (K:) or tEh~dhu and tfq~dhu are used, by some, each in the place of the other; but accord. to Er-Rághib and many others, the former signifies he sought, or sought leisurely or repeatedly, to obtain knowledge of it, having known of it before; and the latter, he sought, or sought leisurely or repeatedly, to obtain knowledge of it, having lost it: (MF in art. fqd :) or tEh~dhu signifies he renewed his acquaintance with it, or his knowledge of it, and sought, or sought leisurely or repeatedly, to find means of rectifying it, reforming it, or putting it into a good or right or proper state: (IDrst, TA:) or he came to it, and rectified it, reformed it, or put it into a good or right or proper state: (Mgh:) or as first expl. above, and also he returned to it time after time, or went frequently to it, and rectified it, reformed it, or put it into a good or right or proper state: (Msb:) or, simply, [as also ↓ tEAhdhu ,] he returned, or recurred, to it time after time, [see an instance voce A^axoraqu ,] or went frequently to it: (Et-Tedmuree, TA:) and also [i. e. both signify also he paid repeated, or frequent, attention to it; or] he was careful, or mindful, of it; or attentive to it. (S, O, Msb. *) One says also, taEah~adotu fulaAnFA [ I renewed my acquaintance with such a one; repaired, or betook myself, to him frequently; paid frequent attention to him; or simply paid attention to him ]. (S, O.) And taEah~adotu DayoEatiY , (S, O, Mgh,) properly signifying I renewed my acquaintance with, or my knowledge of, my estate, is used as meaning I came to my estate, and put it into a good or right or proper condition: (Mgh:) [or I paid repeated, or frequent, or much, attention to it, taking good and effectual care of it; I husbanded it well: ] or, accord. to IDrst, the verb here has the meaning given above on his authority: or, accord. to Ed-Tedmuree, the meaning is that given above as his explanation; and is from EahodN as signifying “ rain that falls after other rain, ” or from the same word as signifying “ a place of abode in which one has known a thing: ” (TA:) and one may say also ↓ taEaAhadotu ; (Fr, ISk, Mgh;) but taEah~adotu is more chaste, (El-Fá- rábee, S, O, Msb,) because ↓ taEaAhudN is only between two [or more]: (S, O:) or tEAhdt is not allowable, (AZ, AHát, Th, IF, Msb,) for the reason just mentioned: (IF, Msb:) AZ says that six Arabs of the desert, of chaste speech, being asked in the presence of himself and of Yoo, one after another, whether they said tEh~dt DyEtY or ↓ tEAhdt , all answered, tEh~dt . (AHát, TA.) One also says, of a man, yataEah~aduhu SaroEN [ Epilepsy befalls him repeatedly, or time after time ]. (S, O.)

definition: [an inf. n. of 1, q. v.: used as a simple subst.,] An injunction, a charge, a bidding, an order, or a command. (S, A, Mgh, O, Msb, K, TA.) [Pl. in this and other senses EuhuwdN .] EahodiY A^ano laA...
sourceDefinition: [an inf. n. of 1, q. v.: used as a simple subst.,] An injunction, a charge, a bidding, an order, or a command. (S, A, Mgh, O, Msb, K, TA.) [Pl. in this and other senses EuhuwdN .] EahodiY A^ano laA A=xu*a mino raADiEK $ayoy^FA , occurring in a trad., is a phrase tropically abridged, meaning (tropical:) It is in the injunction, or charge, prescribed as obligatory on me [ that I should not take anything from a suckling ]. (Mgh.) ― -b2- A compact, a contract, a covenant, an agreement, a confederacy, a league, a treaty, an engagement, a bond, an obligation, or a promise: (S, A, Mgh, O, L, Msb, K, TA:) pl. EuhuwdN : or, accord. to AHeyth, ↓ EahodapN has this this meaning, and EahodN is its pl. [or rather a coll. gen. n.]. (TA.) Hence waliY~u EahodK The suc- cessor by virtue of a covenant of a Khaleefeh [or King]. (TA.) [And wilaAyapu EahodK The succession by virtue of a covenant. ] ― -b3- Protection, or safeguard; a promise, or an assurance, of security or safety; responsibility, or suretiship; syn. A^amaAnN ; and *im~apN ; (Sh, S, A, O, Msb, K;) and DamaAnN ; (O, K;) as also ↓ Euh~ayodaY [in the O ↓ EuhayodaY ] and ↓ EihodaAnN [which last is said in the S and O to be syn. with EahodN , but in what sense is not there specified]. (K.) Hence, *uw EahodK , an appel-lation given to a Christian, and a Jew, [and a Sabian, who is a subject of a Muslim government,] meaning One between whom and the Muslims a compact, or covenant, subsists, whereby the latter are responsible for his security [ and freedom and toleration ] as long as he acts agreeably to the compact [ by living peaceably with them and paying a poll-tax ]; (Mgh, * Msb, * TA;) [i. e. a free non-Muslim subject of a Muslim government; ] as also ↓ muEaAhidN and ↓ muEaAhadN , the act. and pass. forms being both applied to such a person because the compact is mutual; (Msb;) both syn. with *im~iY~N : (S:) persons of this description are called collectively A^aholu AlEahodi . (TA.) ― -b4- An oath: (S, A, O, K:) pl. EuhuwdN : or, accord. to AHeyth, ↓ EahodapN signifies an oath whereby one secures himself against him with whom he makes a compact, contract, covenant, or the like, and EahodN is its pl. [or rather a coll. gen. n.]. (TA.) [But it is generally used as a sing.: hence,] one says, EalaY~a Eahodu A@ll~`hi laA^afoEalan~a ka*aA [ The oath by attestation of God is binding on me that I will assuredly do such a thing ]. (S, O.) ― -b5- A writ, or diploma, of appointment to the office of a prefect or governor or the like: (S, O, K:) pl. EuhuwdN . (TA.) ― -b6- Defence of those persons, or things, that should be sacred, or inviolable, or that are entitled to reverence, respect, honour, or defence; (S, A, O, K;) and mindfulness, regard, or observance, (S, K,) of such things, (K,) or of love, or affection; occurring in this sense in a trad., in which it is said that generosity therein is a point of religion. (S.) ― -b7- Fulfilment of a promise or the like. (O, K.) So in the Kur vii. 100. (O.) ― -b8- The assertion of the unity of God: whence, A_il~aA mani A@t~axa*a Einoda A@lr~aHom`ni EahodFA [ Except such as hath made a covenant with the Compassionate to assert his unity ], (O, K,) in the Kur [xix. 90]: (O:) and the words of a trad. relating to prayer, A^anaA EalaY Eahodika wawaEodika maA A@sotaTaEotu I am persevering in the observance of my covenant and promise to Thee to believe in Thee and to assert thy unity incessantly [ as far as I am able ]. (TA.) -A2- Also A time; (S, * A, K;) and so ↓ EihodaAnN . (A, TA.) One says, kaAna EalaY Eahodi fulaAnK and ↓ EihodaAnihi It was in the time of such a one. (A.) And kaAna *`lika fiY Eahodi $abaAbiY That was in the time of my youth, or young manhood. (TK.) And A^ataY EalayohaA EahodN TawiylN [ Over which a long time has passed ]. (S, in explanation of qaroyapN EahiydapN meaning qadiymapN .) ― -b2- One says also, EahodiY bihi qariybN i. e. My meeting [ with him, or it, was a short time ago ]. (S, * Msb.) And huwa qariybu AlEahodi baka*aA He knew, or was acquainted with, such a thing, and was in such a state, or condition, recently, or a short time ago. (Msb. [And in like manner one says Hadiyvu AlEahodi and Hadiyvu EahodK .]) And EahodiY bihi bimawoDiEi ka*aA , (K, TA,) and fiY HaAli ka*aA , (TA,) I met, or met with, or I knew, [or I saw, ] him, or it, in such a place, (K, TA,) and in such a state, or condition. (TA.) And maA liY EahodN bihi [ I have not any knowledge of, or acquaintance with, him, or it ]. (A.) And mataY Eahoduka bifulaAnK When didst thou meet, or meet with, such a one? (Mgh:) or see such a one? (TA.) And mataY Eahoduka biAlxuf~i When didst thou wear the boots? (Mgh.) And mataY Eahoduka biA^asofali fiyka [ When didst thou see the lower part of thy mouth? ]: a prov.; said in asking a person respecting an old affair of which he has no knowledge. (L.) The saying of the poet, (Aboo-Khirásh El-Hudhalee, TA, and so in a copy of the S,) falayosa kaEahodi Ald~aAri yaA A^um~a maAlikK wal`kino A^aHaATato biAlr~iqaAbi Als~alaAsilu [ And it is not like the formerly-known state of the abode, O Umm-Málik; but chains have surrounded the necks; ] is expl. as meaning, the case is not as thou knewest it; but El-Islám has come, and has subverted that case. (S, TA.) [Hence, liloEahodi and ↓ lilomaEohuwdi , said of the article Aalo ; meaning Used to distinguish a noun as known to the hearer, or reader, in a particular sense. ] -A3- Also A first rain; the rain immediately following which is called waloYN : (TA:) or the first of the rain called AlwasomiY~u ; (IAar, M, K;) and so ↓ EahodapN and ↓ EihodapN and ↓ EihaAdapN , (M, K, TA,) or, as in some copies of the K [and in the CK], ↓ EihaAdN , which is pl. of EahodN . (TA.) ― -b2- And Rain that falls after other rain, (AHn, S, K,) while the moisture of the former yet remains; (AHn, K;) as also ↓ EahodapN and ↓ EihodapN : (TA:) pl. definition: A written statement of a purchase or sale: (S, Msb, K:) so called because one recurs to it on an occasion of doubt.
sourceDefinition: A written statement of a purchase or sale: (S, Msb, K:) so called because one recurs to it on an occasion of doubt. (Msb.) And A written statement of a confederacy, league, compact, or covenant. (K.) ― -b2- Also A return [to claim an indemnification for a fault or the like in a thing purchased]; syn. rajoEapN : so in the saying, laA Euhodapa [ There shall be no return to claim an indemnification]: (S, O, K:) one says, A^abiyEuka AlmalasaY laA Euhodapa i. e. [ I sell to thee on the condition that ] thou shalt get thee away, and not return to me, (S in this art., and S and Msb and K in art. mls ,) nor have any claim upon me for indemnification: (Msb in art. mls :) EuhodapN with respect to an article of merchandise being when it is sold in a faulty state or subject to a claim on the part of its owner. (TA. [See more voce malasaY .]) One says also, Ealayoka fiY h`*ihi EuhodapN laA tatafaS~aY minohaA Thou art subject to a claim for acting unjustly [ in respect of this, from which thou wilt not liberate thyself ]. (A, TA.) And Euhodapu Alr~aqiyqi valaAvapu A^ay~aAmK The claim for indemnification for a fault in a slave, from the property of the seller, if he have sold him without making it a condition that he is clear of responsibility for any fault, is during three days, and the purchaser may return him without proof; but if he find a fault after three days, he may not return him without proof. (TA, from a trad.) And ↓ EahodN and EuhodapN signify the same: (TA:) you say, bariy^otu A_ilayoka mino Euhodapi h`*aA AlEabodi [and ↓ mino Eahodihi ], meaning I am clear of responsibility to thee for any fault that thou mayest find in this slave known to exist in him while he was with me. (AHeyth, Mgh, TA.) See 4. And you say also, Euhodatuhu EalaY fulaAnK The responsibility for the rectification of any fault that may be found in him, or it, is upon such a one. (S, * Mgh, Msb, * K, * TA.) And fiY AlA^amori EuhodapN In the affair is an occasion for reverting to it for the purpose of its rectification; (Msb;) i. e. the affair is not yet performed soundly, thoroughly, or well, (S, O, Msb,) and the manager thereof has to revert to it in order to render it so. (Msb.) And fiyhi EuhodapN In it is a fault, a defect, or an imperfection. (TA.) And fiY Eaqolihi EuhodapN In his intellect is a weakness. (S, A, O, K.) And fiY xaT~ihi EuhodapN In his handwriting is a weakness: (K:) or badness: (A:) or faulty formation of the letters. (O.) -A2- See also EahodapN .

sourceDefinition: signifies The going far into a land, or country; as also ↓ tagoriybN . (K.) And you say, AlkilaAbu ↓ gr~bt The dogs went far in search, or pursuit, of the object, or objects, of the chase. (A, TA.) ― -b2- See also 5. ― -b3- And Agrb signifies He made the place to which he cast, or shot, to be distant, or remote. (A.) ― -b4- Also, (TA,) inf. n. as above, (K, TA,) He (a horse) ran much: (K:) or Agrb fiY jaroyihi , said of a horse, (A, TA,) he exceeded the usual bounds, or degree, in his running: (A:) or he ran at the utmost rate. (TA.) ― -b5- And Agrb fiY AlD~aHiki , (A, K,) and ↓ Aisotagoraba fiyhi , (S, A, * K, *) and ↓ Ausotugoriba (K, TA) i. e. fY AlD~Hk , and DaHikFA ↓ Aisotagoraba occurring in a trad. and Ealayohi AlD~aHiku ↓ Aisotagoraba , and Agrb AlD~aHika , (TA,) He exceeded the usual bounds, or degree, in laughing; (A, K, TA;) or he laughed [ immoderately, or] violently, or vehemently, and much: (S, TA:) or i. q. qahoqaha [q. v.]: (TA:) or Agrb signifies he laughed so that the guruwb [or sharpness and lustre &c.] of his teeth appeared: (L, TA:) or Agrb fY AlDHk means he exceeded the usual bounds, or degree, in laughing, so that his eye shed tears [which are sometimes termed garob ]. (Har p. 572.) In the saying, in a certain form of prayer, ↓ A^aEuw*u bika mino kul~i $ayoTaAnK musotagoribK [ I seek protection by Thee from every devil &c.], the meaning of mstgrb is thought by El-Harbee to be exorbitant in evilness, wickedness, or the like; as though from AlAisotigoraAbu fiY AlD~aHiki : or it may mean sharp, or vehement, in the utmost degree. (TA.) ― -b6- And Agrb , (S, Msb,) inf. n. as above, (K,) He did, or said, what was strange, or extraordinary. (S, Msb, K.) You say, takal~ama faA^agoraba He spoke, and said what was strange, and used extraordinary words: and yugoribu fiY kalaAmihi [ He uses strange, or extraordinary, words in his speech ]. (A, TA.) ― -b7- Also, (TA,) inf. n. as above, (K,) He came to the west. (K, TA.) [See also 2.] -A2- Agrb also signifies He had a white child born to him. (TA.) ― -b2- And A_igoraAbN signifies Whiteness of the groins, (K, TA,) next the flank. (TA.) You say, of a man, Agrb meaning He was white in his groins. (TK.) -A3- See also garabN . -A4- Agrb as trans.: see 2. ― -b2- A_igoraAbN said of a rider signifies His making his horse to run until he dies: (K:) or, accord. to Fr, one says, AErb EalaY farasihi meaning “ he made his horse to run: ” [or AErb farasahu has this meaning: (see 4 in art. Erb :)] but he adds that some say Agrb . (O in art. Erb .) ― -b3- And Agrb , (S, TA,) inf. n. as above, (K, TA,) He filled (S, K, TA) a skin, (S, TA,) and a watering-trough or tank, and a vessel. (TA.) Bishr (Ibn-Abee-Kházim, TA) says, wakaA^an~a ZuEonahumu gadaApa taHam~aluwA ↓ sufunN takaf~aA^u fiY xaliyjK mugorabi [ And as though their women's camel-vehicles, on the morning when they bound the burdens on their beasts and departed, were ships inclining forwards (or moving from side to side like the tall palm-tree ) in a filled river (or canal )]. (TA.) ― -b7- And A^ugoriba said of a horse, His blaze spread (S, K) so that it took in his eyes, and the edges of his eyelids were white: and it is used in like manner to signify that they were white by reason of what is termed zaraqN [inf. n. of zariqa , q. v.]. (S, TA.) See its part. n., mugorabN .

sourceDefinition: [an inf. n. of garaba , q. v., in several senses. ― -b2- As a simple subst.,] Distance, or remoteness; and so ↓ garobapN . (A, K.) Aln~awaY ↓ garobapu [in one of my copies of the S gurobap ] means The distance, or remoteness, of the place which one purposes to reach in his journey. (S, TA.) ― -b3- [And hence, used as an epithet, Distant, or remote. ] You say nawFY garobapN [in one of my copies of the S gurobapN ] A distant, or remote, place which one purposes to reach in his journey. (S, A. *) And daAru fulaAnK garobapN The house, or abode, of such a one is distant, or remote. (TA.) And daraAhimu garobapN Distant money [so that it is not easily attainable ]. (TA.) And EayonN garobapN A far-seeing eye: and A_in~ahu lagarobu AlEayoni Verily he is far-seeing; and of a woman you say garobapu AlEayoni . (TA.) -A2- And Algarobu is syn. with ↓ Almagoribu , (S, M, Msb, K,) which latter is also pronounced ↓ Almagorabu , with fet-h to the r , but more commonly with kesr, (Msb,) or accord. to analogy it should be with fet-h, but usage has given it kesr, as in the case of Alma$oriqu ; (TA;) [both signify The west; ] Algarobu is the contr. of Al$~aroqu ; (M, TA;) and ↓ Almagoribu [is the contr. of Alma$oriqu , and] originally signifies the place [or point ] of sunset, (TA,) as also Al$~amosi ↓ magoribaAnu ; (K;) and is likewise used to signify the time of sunset; and also as an inf. n.: (TA:) and ↓ AlmagoribaAni signifies the two places [or points ] where the sun sets; i. e. the furthest [or northernmost ] place of sunset in summer [W. 26 degrees N. in Central Arabia] and the furthest [or southernmost ] place of sunset in winter [W. 26 degrees S. in Central Arabia]: (T, TA:) between these two points are a hundred and eighty points, every one of which is called magoribN ; and so between the two points called Alma$oriqaAni . (TA.) -A3- garobN signifies also The first part (S, K) of a thing (K) [and particularly] (assumed tropical:) of the run of a horse. (S.) ― -b2- And The Had~ [or edge ] (S, K) of a thing, as also ↓ guraAbN , (K,) or of a sword and of anything; (S;) and thus [particularly] the ↓ guraAb of the faA^os [or adz, &c.]. (S, K.) ― -b3- And (assumed tropical:) Sharpness (S, A, Msb, TA) of a sword, (TA,) or of anything, such as the faA^os [or adz, &c.], and of the knife, (Msb,) and (Msb, TA) (assumed tropical:) of the tongue: (S, A, Msb, TA:) and [as meaning (assumed tropical:) sharpness of temper or the like, passionateness, irritability, or vehemence, ] of a man, (TA,) and of a horse, (S, TA,) and of youth: (A, TA:) [from the same word signifying the “ edge ” of a sword &c.: whence the saying, A^arohifo garoba *ihonika lamaA A^aquwlu (mentioned in the A and TA in art. Arhf ) meaning (tropical:) Sharpen the edge of thine intellect for what I say: ] and ↓ garobapN signifies the same. (TA.) And Vehemence of might or strength, or of valour or prowess, of men; syn. $awokapN . (TA.) [And hence, app., (assumed tropical:) Briskness, liveliness, or sprightliness: and (assumed tropical:) perseverance in an affair: see the first paragraph.] ― -b4- Also, [used as an epithet,] (assumed tropical:) Sharp, applied to a sword [and the like], and to a tongue. (TA.) And, applied to a horse, (assumed tropical:) That runs much: (S, K:) or that casts himself forward, with uninterrupted running, not desisting until he has gone far with his ride. (TA.) -A4- And A large dalow [or leathern bucket ], (S, Mgh, Msb, K, TA,) made of a bull's hide, (Mgh, TA,) with which one draws water on the [ camel, or she-camel, called ] saAniyap [q. v.]: (Msb:) of the masc. gender: pl. guruwbN . (TA.) So expl. in the following words of a trad.: A^axa*a Ald~alowa Eumaru faA@sotaHaAlato garobFA [ 'Omar took the dlw , and it became changed into a grb ]; i. e. when he took the dlw to draw water, it became large in his hand: for the conquests in his time were more than those in the time of Aboo-Bekr. (IAth, TA.) ― -b2- And A [ camel, or any beast, such as is called ] raAwiyap , (K, TA,) upon which water is carried. (TA.) ― -b3- And accord. to the K, A day of irrigation: but [this is app. a mistake: for] Az says that Lth has mentioned the phrase fiY yawomi garobK , meaning thereby in a day in which water is drawn with the [ large bucket called ] garob , [ for irrigation, ] on the [ camel, or she-camel, called ] saAniyap . (TA.) -A5- And Tears (K, TA) when they come forth from the eye: (TA:) or guruwbN signifies tears; (S;) and is pl. of garobN . (TA.) A poet says, maA laka laA ta*okuru A^um~a Eamoriw A_il~aA liEayonayoka guruwbN tajoriY [ What aileth thee, that thou dost not mention Umm-'Amr but thine eyes have tears flowing? ]. (S, TA.) And it is said of Ibn-'Abbás, in a trad., kaAna mivaj~FA yasiylu garobFA i. e. (tropical:) [ He was an eloquent orator, flowing with ] a copious and uninterrupted stream of knowledge, likened to garob as meaning “ tears coming forth from the eye. ” (TA.) ― -b2- And A flowing, ( masiylN , K,) or vehement flowing, ( AinohilaAlN , A, K,) in one copy of the K AinohimaAlN [which means a flowing ], (TA,) of tears from the eye: (A, K:) and a single flow ( fayoDapN ) of tears, and of wine. (K.) ― -b3- And A certain vein, or duct, ( EiroqN ,) in the channel of the tears, (S, Mgh,) or in the eye, (A, K,) that flows [ with tears ] uninterruptedly; (S, A, Msb, K;) like what is termed naAsuwrN . (S, Mgh.) One says of a person whose tears flow without intermission, baEayonihi garobN . (As, S, Mgh.) And [the pl.] Alguruwbu signifies The channels of the tears. (S.) ― -b4- Also The inner angle of the eye, and the outer angle thereof. (S, A, K.) ― -b5- And A tumour in the inner angles of the eyes; (Mgh, K;) as also ↓ garabN . (Mgh.) ― -b6- And A pustule ( bavorapN ) in the eye, (K, TA,) which discharges blood, and the bleeding of which will not be stopped. (TA.) ― -b7- And Abundance of saliva (K, TA) in the mouth; (TA;) and the moisture thereof, i. e., of saliva: (K:) pl. guruwbN . (TA.) And The place where the saliva collects and remains: (K, TA:) or the garob in a tooth is the place where the saliva thereof collects and remains: (TA:) or garobN , (TA,) or its pl. guruwbN , (S, TA,) signifies the sharpness, and maA=' [meaning lustre ], (S, TA,) of the tooth, (TA,) or of the teeth: (S, TA:) accord. to the T and M and Nh and L, guruwbu AlA^asonaAni signifies the places where the saliva of the teeth collects and remains: or, as some say, their extremities and sharpness and maA=' [which may here mean either water or lustre ]: or the maA=' that runs upon the teeth: (TA:) or their maA=' , and shining whiteness: (A, TA:) or their fineness, or thinness, and sharpness: or guruwbN signifies the sharp, or serrated, edges of the fore teeth: it is also, as pl. of garobN , expl. as signifying the maA=' of the fam [by which may be meant either the water of the mouth or the lustre of the teeth, for Alfamu properly signifies “ the mouth ” and metonymically “ the teeth ”], and the sharpness of the teeth: and accord. to MF, as on the authority of the Nh, [but SM expresses a doubt as to its correctness,] it is also applied to the teeth [themselves]. (TA.) [See also $anabN , in two places.] -A6- A^aSaAbahu sahomu garobK and ↓ sahomu garabK , and sahomN garobN and ↓ sahomN garabN , (S, Msb, * K,) the second of which, i. e. ↓ sahomu garabK , accord. to IKt, is the most approved, (MF,) mean An arrow of which the shooter was not known [ struck him ]: (S, Msb, K:) or, accord. to some, shm garob signifies an arrow from an unknown quarter; shm ↓ garab , an arrow that is shot and that strikes another. (TA.) -A7- And garobN signifies also A certain tree of El-Hijáz, (K, TA,) green, (TA,) large, or thick, and thorny, (K, TA,) whence is made [or prepared ] the kuHayol [i. e. tar ] with which [ mangy ] camels are smeared: [or it is a coll. gen. n., for] its n. un. is with p : so says ISd: kHyl is qaTiraAn , of the dial. of El-Hijáz: and he [app. ISd] says also, the A^abohal [q. v.] is the same as the garob , because qTrAn is extracted from it. (TA.) Hence, as some say, (K, TA,) the trad., (TA,) laA yazaAlu A^aholu Algarobi ZaAhiriyna EalaY AlHaq~i [ The people of the grb will not cease to be attainers of the truth, or of the true religion ]: (K, TA:) or the meaning is, the people of Syria, because Syria is [a little to the] west of El-Hijáz: or the people of sharpness, and of vehemence of might or strength, or of valour or prowess; i. e. the warriors against unbelievers: or the people of the bucket called garob ; i. e. the Arabs: or the people of the west; which meaning is considered by Iyád and others the most probable, because, in the relation of the trad. by Ed-Dárakutnee, the word in question is Almagorib . (L, TA.)

(TA.) Hence, as some say, (K, TA,) the trad., (TA,) laA yazaAlu A^aholu Algarobi ZaAhiriyna EalaY AlHaq~i [ The people of the grb will not cease to be attainers of the truth, or of the true religion ]: (K, TA:) or the meaning is, the people of Syria, because Syria is [a little to the] west of El-Hijáz: or the people of sharpness, and of vehemence of might or strength, or of valour or prowess; i. e. the warriors against unbelievers: or the people of the bucket called garob ; i. e. the Arabs: or the people of the west; which meaning is considered by Iyád and others the most probable, because, in the relation of the trad. by Ed-Dárakutnee, the word in question is Almagorib . (L, TA.)

definition: Silver: or a [ vessel such as is termed ] jaAm of silver;
sourceDefinition: Silver: or a [ vessel such as is termed ] jaAm of silver; (S, K;) [i. e.] a [ drinking-cup or bowl such as is termed ] qadaH of silver. (L, TA.) A poet says, fadaEodaEaA sur~apa Alr~akaA='i kamaA daEodaEa saAqiY AlA^aEaAjimi AlgarabaA cited in the S as being by El-Aashà but it is said in the L, IB says, this verse is by Lebeed, not by El-Aashà, describing two torrents meeting together; meaning, And they filled the middle of the valley of Er-Rehà, also, but less correctly, called Er-Rikà, like as the cup-bearer of the AEAjm [or foreigners ] fills the silver qadaH with wine: the verse of El-Aashà in which [it is said that] garab occurs as meaning “ silver ” is, A_i*aA A@nokab~a A^azoharu bayona Als~uqaApi taraAmawoA bihi garabFA wanuDaAraA i. e. When a white wine-jug is turned down so as to pour out its contents [ among the cup-bearers ], they hand it, i. e. the wine in the cups, one to another [while it resembles silver or gold ]: (L, TA:) garabFA is here in the accus. case as a denotative of state, though signifying a substance: [and so nuDaAraA :] but it is said that garabN and nuDaArN signify species of trees from which are made [drinkingcups or bowls such as are termed] A^aqodaAH [pl. of qadaHN ]: and it is said in the T that nuDaArN signifies a species of trees from which are made yellow A^aqodaAH . (TA.) ― -b2- [In explanation of the last of the applications of garabN mentioned above, it is said that] it signifies also A species of trees (T, S, ISd, TA) from which are made white [ drinking-cups or bowls of the kind termed ] A^aqodaAH ; (T, TA;) called in Pers. A_isbiydo daAr [or A_isoPiydaAr ]: (S:) [generally held to mean the willow; like the Hebr. עֲרָבִים ; or particularly the species called salix Babylonica: a coll. gen. n.:] n. un. with p . (ISd, TA.) [Avicenna (Ibn-Seenà), in book ii. p. 279, mentions a tree called grb , but describes only the uses and supposed properties of its bark &c., particularizing its Samog ; whence it appears that he means the garob , not the garab .] ― -b3- It also signifies A [ vessel of the kind termed ] qadaH [perhaps such as is made from the species of trees above mentioned]: (K, TA:) and its pl. is A^agoraAbN . (TA.) ― -b4- And Gold. (K.) ― -b5- And Wine. (S, K.) ― -b6- And The water that drops from the buckets between the well and the watering-trough or tank, (S, K,) and which soon alters in odour: (S:) or any water that pours from the buckets from about the mouth of the well to the wateringtrough or tank, and that soon alters in odour: or the water and mud that are around the well and the watering-trough or tank: (TA:) and (as some say, TA) the odour of water and mud: (K:) so called because it soon alters. (TA.) [Hence] one says, lA tgrb , [thus in the TA, so that it may be ↓ lA tagorubo or ↓ lA tugar~ibo or ↓ lA tugoribo ,] meaning Spill not thou the water between the well and the watering-trough or tank, so as to make mud. (TA.) -A2- Also A certain disease in sheep or goats, (S, K,) like the saEaf in the she-camel, in consequence of which the hair of the xuroTuwm [i. e. nose, or fore part of the nose, ] and that of the eyes fall off. (S.) ― -b2- And [ A colour such as is termed ] zaraq [q. v.] in the eye of a horse, (K, TA,) together with whiteness thereof. (TA.) ― -b3- See also garobN , latter half, in five places.

definition: One of the most excellent kinds of grapes;
sourceDefinition: One of the most excellent kinds of grapes; (K;) a sort of grapes growing at Et-Táïf, in- tensely black, of the most exceuent, and most delicate, and blackest, of grapes. (TA.) [See an ex. in a verse cited voce EajiybapN .] ― -b2- Applied to an old man, Intensely black [app. in the hair ]: or whose hair does not become white, or hoary: (TA:) or, so applied, who blackens his white, or hoary, hair with dye: (K, TA:) occurring in a trad., in which it is said that God hates such an old man: pl. garaAbiybu . (TA.) ― -b3- A^asowadu girobiybN means Intensely black: but if you say garaAbiybu suwdN , you make the latter word a substitute for the former; because a word corroborative of one signifying a colour cannot precede; (S, K;) nor can the corroborative of any word: (Suh, MF:) or, accord. to Hr, garaAbiybu suwdN [in the Kur xxxv. 25], relating to mountains, means Streaks having black rocks. (TA.)

definition: A certain black bird, (TA,) well known;
sourceDefinition: A certain black bird, (TA,) well known; (K, TA;) [the corvus, or crow; ] of which there are several species; [namely, the raven, carrioncrow, rook, jackdaw, jay, magpie, &c.:] and it was used as a proper name, which, as is said in a trad., he [i. e. Mohammad] changed, because the word implies the meaning of distance, and because it is the name of a foul bird: (TA:) the pl. [of mult.] is girobaAnN (S, Msb, K) and gurobN (K) and (of pauc., S) A^agoribapN (S, Msb, K) and A^agorubN ; (Msb, K;) and pl. pl. garaAbiynu . (K.) When the Arabs characterize a land as fertile, they say, waqaEa fiY A^aroDK laA yuTay~aru guraAbuhaA (tropical:) [ He lighted upon a land of which the crow will not be made to fly away; because of its abundant herbage: see also Tay~ara ]: and wajada vamarapa AlguraAbi (assumed tropical:) [ He found the fruit of the crow ]; because that bird seeks after and chooses the most excellent of fruits. (TA.) They also say, TaAra guraAbu fulaAnK (tropical:) [ The crow of such a one flew away ], meaning the head of such a one became white, or hoary. (A, TA. [See also a similar phrase below.]) Also, fulaAnN A^aboSaru mino guraAbK [ Such a one is more sharp-sighted than a crow ]: and A^aHo*aru [ more cautious ]: and A^azohaY [ more proud ]: and A^a$oA^amu [ more inauspicious ]: &c.: they say that this bird is more inauspicious than any other inauspicious thing upon the earth. (TA.) In the phrase ↓ guraAbN gaAribN , the epithet is added to give intensiveness to the signification. (TA.) guraAbu Albayoni has been expl. in art. byn . ― -b2- AlguraAbu is the name of (assumed tropical:) One of the southern constellations, [i. e. Corvus, ] consisting of seven stars [ in the enumeration of Ptolemy ], behind AlbaATiyap [which is Crater ], to the south of Als~imaAku AlA^aEozalu [i. e. Spica Virginis ]. (Kzw.) ― -b3- A^agoribapu AlEarabi is an appellation of (assumed tropical:) The blacks [lit. crows ] of the Arabs; the black Arabs: (K, TA:) likened to the birds called Agrbp , in respect of their complexion: (TA:) in all of them the blackness was derived from their mothers. (MF, TA.) The A^agoribap in the Time of Ignorance were 'Antarah and Khufáf Ibn-Nudbeh (asserted to have been a Mukhadram, TA) and Aboo-'Omeyr Ibn-El- Hobáb and Suleyk Ibn-Es-Sulakeh (a famous runner, TA) and Hishám Ibn-'Okbeh-Ibn-AbeeMo'eyt; but this last was a Mukhadram: and those among the Islámees, 'Abd-Allah Ibn-Khá- zim and 'Omeyr Ibn-Abee-'Omeyr and Hemmám [in the CK Humám] Ibn-Mutarrif and Munteshir Ibn-Wahb and Matar Ibn-Abee-Owfà and Taäbbata-Sharrà and Esh-Shenfarà and Hájiz; to the last of whom is given no appellation of the kind called “ nisbeh, ” (K, TA,) in relation to father, mother, tribe, or place. (TA.) ― -b4- rijolu AlguraAbi signifies (assumed tropical:) A certain herb, called in the language of the Barbar A_iToriylaAl , (K, TA,) and in the present day zir~u AlA^axil~api , (MF,) resembling the $ibiv~ [q. v., variously written in different copies of the K,] in its stem and in its jum~ap [or node whence the flower grows ] and in its lower part, or root, except that its flower is white, and it forms grains like those of the maqoduwnis [app. scandix cerefolium or apium petroselinum ], (K, TA,) nearly: (TA:) a drachm of its seeds, bruised, and mixed with honey (K, TA) deprived of its froth, (TA,) is a tried medicine for eradicating [the species of leprosy which are called] the baraS and the bahaq , being drunk; and sometimes is added to it a quarter of a drachm of EaAqiro qaroHaA , (K, TA,) which is [commonly] known by the name of Ewd AlqrH [i. e. Euwdu AlqaroHi , both of these being names now applied to pyrethrum, i. e. pellitory of Spain, but the latter, accord. to Forskål (Flora Ægypt. Arab. p. cxix.), applied in El-Yemen to the cacalia sonchifolia, or to a species of senecio]; (TA;) the patient sitting in a hot sun, with the diseased parts uncovered: (K, TA:) [see also rijolN : now applied to the chelidonium hybridum of Linn., chelidonium dodecandrum of Forsk.: (Delile's Floræ Ægypt. Illustr. no. 502:) in Bocthor's Dict. Français-Arabe, both the names of rjl AlgrAb and ATrylAl are given to the plants called cerfeuil (or chervil ) and corne de cerf (or buck'shorn plantain, also called coronopus ).] ― -b5- Also (i. e. rijolu AlguraAbi ) A certain mode of binding the udder of a camel, (S, K,) tightly, (S,) so that the young one cannot suck; (K;) nor will it undo. (TA.) [Hence] one says, Sur~a Ealayohi rijolu AlguraAbi , meaning (tropical:) The affair was, or became, difficult, or strait, to him: (A, * K:) or his life, or subsistence, was, or became, so. (TA.) sourceDefinition: (S, Msb, K) and ↓ gurubN (S, K) and ↓ gariybiY~N (AA, TA) signify the same, (S, K, TA,) [ A stranger, or foreigner; ] one far, or distant, from his home, or native country; (Msb;) a man not of one's own people: (TA:) a man not of one's own kindred; an alien with respect to kindred; (S in explanation of the first;) pl. of the first gurabaA='u ; (S, TA;) and gurobN [also] is a pl. of gariybN , like as qurobN is of qariybN : (TA in art. zlf :) fem. of the first gariybapN ; pl. garaAy^ibu . (L, TA.) A^a*aAEato gazolahaA fiY AlgaraAy^ibi , a phrase used by a poet, means She distributed her thread among the strange women: for most of the women who spin for hire are strangers. (L, TA.) And one says wajohN kamiroA=pi Algariybapi [ A face like the mirror of her who is a stranger ]: because, the gariybap being among such as are not her own people, her mirror is always polished; for she has none to give her a sincere opinion respecting her face. (A.) And laA^aDoriban~akumo Daroba gariybapi AlA_ibili (tropical:) [ I will assuredly beat you with the beating of the strange one of the camels ] is a saying of El-Hajjáj threatening the subjects of his government; meaning, as a strange camel, intruding among others when they come to water, is beaten and driven away. (IAth, TA.) And [hence] qidoHN gariybN means (assumed tropical:) [ An arrow, without feathers or head, ] such as is not of the same trees whereof are the rest of the arrows. (TA.) ― -b2- gariybN signifies also Language that is strange; [ unusual, extraordinary, or unfamiliar; ] far from being intelligible; difficult to be understood; or obscure. (Msb, TA.) Hence, muSan~afu Algariybi [ The composition on the subject of the strange kind of words &c. ]. (A, TA.) [Hence also AlgariybaAni The two classes of strange words &c., namely, those occurring in the Kur-án, and those of the Traditions.] And kalimapN gariybapN A word, or an expression, that is [ strange, &c., or] obscure: (A, TA:) gariybapN applied to a word [and often used as an epithet in which the quality of a subst. is predominant] is opposed to faSiyHapN : and its pl. is garaAy^ibu . (Mz 13th nwE .) ― -b3- [And hence it often signifies Improbable. ] ― -b4- Applied to a trad., it means Traced up uninterruptedly to the Apostle of God, but related by only one person. of the taAbiEuwna or of those termed A^atobaAEu Alt~aAbiEiyna or of those termed A^atobaAEu A^atobaAEi Alt~aAbiEiyna . (KT.) -A2- [The fem.] gariybapN , in a verse of Aboo-Kebeer El-Hudhalee, as some relate it, is expl. by Skr as meaning Black; syn. sawodaA='u . (TA voce Eaziyzapu [q. v. It is perhaps used by poetic license for girobiybapN , fem. of girobiybN .])

definition: [The western side of a mountain &c.
sourceDefinition: [The western side of a mountain &c.]. You say, h`*aA gaAribu Aljabali and ↓ garobiy~uhu [ This is the western side of the mountain ], and [in the opposite sense] h*A $aAriqu Aljabali and $aroqiy~uhu . (TA in art. $rq .) -A2- Also The kaAhil [or withers ], (A, K, TA,) of the camel; (TA;) or the part between the hump and the neck; (S, A, Msb, K, TA;) upon which the leading-rope is thrown when the camel is sent to pasture where he will: (Msb:) pl. gawaAribu . (Msb, K.) ― -b2- Hence the saying, (S, &c.,) Haboluki EalaY gaAribiki [ Thy rope is upon thy withers ]; (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K, TA;) used (Msb, TA) by the Arabs in the Time of Ignorance (TA) in divorcing; (Msb, TA;) meaning (tropical:) I have left thy way free, or open, to thee; (TA;) go whithersoever thou wilt: (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K, TA:) originating from the fact of throwing a she-camel's leading-rope upon her withers, if it is upon her, when she pastures; for when she sees the leading-rope, nothing is productive of enjoyment to her. (As, S, TA.) ― -b3- AlgaAribaAni signifies The fore and kind parts of the back [and of the hump ]: and baEiyrN *uw gaAribayoni , A camel whereof the part between the gArbAn [or fore and kind parts ] of the hump is cleft; which is mostly the case in the baxaAtiY~ , whose sire is the faAlij [or large twohumped camel of Es-Sind] and his dam Arabian. (TA.) ― -b4- And gaAribN signifies also The fore part of the hump: thus in the following saying, in a trad. of Ez-Zubeyr: famaA zaAla yafotilu fiY Al*~irowapi waAlgaAribi Hat~aY A^ajaAbatohu EaAy^i$apu A_ilaY Alxuruwji i. e. (assumed tropical:) [ And he ceased not to twist the fur of] the upper part and the fore part of the hump [ until 'Áïsheh gave him her consent to go forth ]; meaning, he ceased not to practise guile with her, and to wheedle her, until she gave hun her consent: originating from the fact that, when a man desires to render a refractory camel tractable, and to attach to him the nose-rein, he passes his hand over him, and strokes his gArb , and twists its fur, until he has become familiar: (L, TA:) or gaAribN signifies the upper portion of the fore part of the hump. (Lth, TA.) ― -b5- Also (tropical:) The upper part of a wave: (Lth, TA:) gawaAribu AlmaA='i means (tropical:) the higher parts of the waves of water; (S, K, TA;) likened to the gwArb of camels: (S, TA:) or the higher parts of water. sourceDefinition: and mugar~abN [ A term, or limit, &c.,] distant, or remote. (S.) ― -b2- And xayarN mugar~ibN Fresh, or recent, information, or news, from a foreign, or strange, land or country. (TA.) One says, halo jaA='akumo mugar~ibapu xabarK Has any information, or news, come to you from a foreign, or strange, land or country? (Yaakoob, S, TA:) and halo mino mugar~ibapi xabarK (A'Obeyd, A, Msb, TA) and mugar~abapi xabarK (A'Obeyd, Msb, TA) Is there any information from a distant place? (A;) or any occasion of such information? (Msb;) or any new information from a distant land or country? or, accord. to Th, mgr~bp xbr means new, or recent, information. (TA.) [See an ex. voce junubN : and see also muqar~ibN .] ― -b3- Almugar~ibuwna , mentioned in a trad., (Hr, Nh, K, TA,) in which it is said, A_in~a fiykumo mugar~ibiyna , (Hr, Nh, TA,) is expl. [app. by Mohammad] as meaning Those in whom the jinn [or demons ] have a partnership, or share: so called because a foreign strain has entered into them, or because of their coming from a remote stock: (Hr, Nh, K, TA:) and by the jinn's having a partnership, or share, in them, is said to be meant their bidding them to commit adultery, or fornication, and making this to seem good to them; so that their children are unlawfully begotten: this expression being similar to one in the Kur xvii. 66. (Nh, TA.) ― -b4- And mugar~ibN signifies also One going, or who goes, to, or towards, the west. (S.) [See an ex. voce mu$ar~iqN .]

definition: A small drinking-cup or bowl, (S, K,) with which people divided the water among themselves in a journey when they had little of it;
sourceDefinition: A small drinking-cup or bowl, (S, K,) with which people divided the water among themselves in a journey when they had little of it; and this they [sometimes] did by putting a pebble into a vessel, and then pouring into it as much water as would cover the pebble, and giving it to each man among them: (TA:) or the smallest of drinking-cups or bowls: (K:) [see qaEobN ; and tibonN :] accord. to ISh, it contains twice or thrice the quantity of the measure called kiylajap : [but this seems to be a large gmr , used for watering a horse; and the words which here immediately follow are app. not added by ISh, but relate to the gmr used by a man for himself or for another man:] the qaEob is larger than it, and satisfies the thirst of a man: the pl. is A^agomaArN . (TA.) El-Aashà of Báhileh says, in an elegy on his brother ElMunteshir Ibn-Wahb, takofiyhi Huz~apu filo*K A_ino A^alom~a bihaA mina Al$~iwaA='i wayurowiY $urobahu Algumaru [ A slice of camel's liver, roasted, if he lighted upon it, used to suffice him; and the gumar used to satisfy his thirst ]. (S, TA.) And Mohammad is related, in a trad., to have said, laA tajoEaluwniY kagumari Alr~aAkibi Sal~uwA EalaY A^aw~ala Ald~uEaA='i waA^awosaTahu waA=xirahu Make ye me not like the gumar of the rider: salute me in the beginning of prayer and in the middle thereof and in the end thereof: meaning that they should not make the salutation of him to be a thing of no great importance, and to be postponed: for the rider puts on his camel his saddle and his travel-ling-provisions, and last of all hangs upon his saddle his drinking-cup. (IAth, TA.)

definition: Water that rises above the stature of a man.
sourceDefinition: Water that rises above the stature of a man. (Bd in xxiii. 56.) See also gamorN , first sentence. ― -b2- Hence, (Bd,) fa*arohumo fiY gamoratihimo , in the Kur xxiii. 56, (tropical:) Therefore leave thou them in [ the submerging gulf, or flood, of ] their ignorance; (Fr, Bd;) or in their error: (Jel:) or in their error and obstinacy and perplexity: (Zj, in explanation of another reading, fY gamaraAtihimo :) and in like manner, fiY gamorapN , in the same chap., verse 65, signifies in overwhelming heedlessness: (Bd:) or in ignorance: (Jel:) and in the Kur li. 11, in overwhelming ignorance: (Bd, Jel:) or gamorapN signifies [here] a state of obstinate perseverance in vain or false affairs: (Lth, Msb, TA:) and gamaraAtN is the pl. (Msb.) You say huwa fiY gamorapK mino lahowK , and $abiybapK , and sukorK , (tropical:) [ He is in a submerging gulf, or flood, of frivolous diversion, and of youthful folly, and of intoxication ]. (TA.) And gamaraAtu jahan~ama signifies [ The fiery depths of Hell; or] the places, of Hell, that abound with fire. (TA.) ― -b3- [Hence] gamorapu AlxuSuwmapi (assumed tropical:) The main part of the contention. (TA.) [And gamorapu AlHarobi (assumed tropical:) The main part, i. e. the thick, or thickest, of the fight or battle. (See also gamaraAtu AlHarobi in what follows.)] ― -b4- Hence likewise, gamorapN signifies also (tropical:) Difficulty, trouble, distress, or rigour, (S, Msb, K,) and pressure, of a thing: (K:) pl. gamaraAtN (S, Msb, K) and gimaArN (K) and gumarN . (S.) Hence, (Msb,) gamaraAtu Almawoti (tropical:) The rigours, or pangs, ( $adaAy^idu ,) of death: (S, Msb:) or gamorapu Almawoti signifies the agony, i. e. the vehemence of the troubles or disquietudes, of death: (TA:) and gamaraAtu AlHarobi , and gimaAruhaA , (assumed tropical:) the rigours of war. (TA.) ― -b5- See also gamorN again, latter half, in three places.
